title: Borrowing: How Languages Take Words
text:
Journal (5 min)
Choose one and write silently.


Option A
Pick a word you use every day that you know (or suspect) came from another language. What language? Why do you think it came in?

Option B
Do you ever mix languages when you talk with family or friends? What does it sound like? Is it the same as using a borrowed word?


~5 min: 4 min writing, then 1-2 volunteers. Option B is a setup for the borrowing vs. code-switching distinction (Geraghty, p. 165). Students who speak Pidgin, Hawaiian, or another language at home are experts here; don’t cold-call.
ANSWERS / SAMPLE RESPONSES: Option A: common answers are food and everyday words (ketchup, sushi, kimchi, taboo, tsunami, aloha, mahalo, shoyu); they usually came in with a new thing, a new food, or contact through trade, migration, or colonization. Option B: mixing languages mid-conversation is code-switching, which requires both speakers to know both languages; a borrowed word is a word that has become part of one language and is used even by people who don’t speak the donor language (see the code-switching slide).

title: Borrowing: How Languages Take Words
text:
Borrowing: Language Features Move
Languages change from the inside (natural change) and by acquiring features from other languages. The second way is borrowing (also called “copying”). Borrowed features are loans.








Type
Example
Source




Sound
[ʒ] in pleasure, beige, rouge
French (Middle English period)


Word
Honolulu in English; pipi ‘cattle’ in Hawaiian
Hawaiian; English beef


Word ending
-s in he sits, replacing -eth
Old Norse


Sentence structure
Hawaiian i luna o ke Kīnaʻu (‘on board the Kinau’)
English


Meaning (calque)
Fijian raica cake (‘look upwards at’) now means ‘respect’
English look up to




Clue to a loan: [ʒ] is rare in English and never starts a word. Odd sounds can give away outside origin.


Geraghty, pp. 165-166. Borrowing can occur in all domains: phonological, lexical, morphological, syntactic, semantic, and pragmatic. Footnote 1: Lynch, Ross, and Crowley (2002) prefer “copying.” French loans also made [v] and [z] full phonemes of English. Also in the chapter: the missionaries tried to add /b d r s t/ to Hawaiian; speakers did not accept them (raisi ‘rice’ is pronounced /laiki/). Ship names: Kīnaʻu went from a proper noun to a common noun with the article ke.

title: Borrowing: How Languages Take Words
text:
Borrowing or Code-Switching?
Code-switching = bilinguals switching languages when talking to other bilinguals. It is not borrowing.

Ua hana mākou me ka wikiwiki real fast kind. ‘We did it very quickly without much care.’ (Hawaiian with English)

In pairs. For each, decide: loan or code-switch? What’s your evidence?

English speakers say Honolulu in an English sentence
Two bilinguals switch to Spanish for a whole sentence
A Pidgin speaker says Pau hana, we go kaukau
A Hawaiian speaker says kelepona (‘telephone’)


Test ideas: Do monolinguals use it? Is it adapted to the recipient language’s sounds and grammar? Is it used consistently?


Geraghty, p. 165, footnote 2 gives the Hawaiian-English example. The tests are my addition (standard in contact linguistics). Answers: 1 loan (monolingual English speakers use it); 2 code-switch; 3 pau hana and kaukau are established loans in Pidgin; the sentence is Pidgin; 4 loan (adapted to Hawaiian sounds; kelepona is one of the chapter’s direct loans, p. 169). Accept debate: the line is a continuum.

title: Borrowing: How Languages Take Words
section: Why Does English Have Both Cow and Beef?
text:
Why Does English Have Both Cow and Beef?
Look at the animal and the meat:


On the farm

cow
pig
sheep
calf
deer


On the plate

beef
pork
mutton
veal
venison



Think first: Why would one language have two different sets of words for the same animals? And what about chicken?


Click once to reveal the “on the plate” column. Let students guess before revealing. Pair them: cow/beef, pig/pork, sheep/mutton, calf/veal, deer/venison. Geraghty, p. 167 lists pork, beef, mutton as the example. The extra pairs (calf/veal, deer/venison) are standard English etymology, from French veau and venaison. Do not tell them the answer yet: ask where the “meat” words look like they come from.
ANSWER (reveal on the next slide): English has two sets because two languages and two social classes met after the Norman conquest of 1066. English-speaking peasants tended the animals and kept the English words; the French-speaking elite ate the meat and used French-derived words. Chicken is not a French/English pair: chicken is English for both the bird and the meat, and French-derived poultry names the group.

title: Borrowing: How Languages Take Words
text:
The Answer: 1066 and Two Classes


Who did what after the Norman conquest

English speakers (peasants) raised the animals, using English words: cow, pig, sheep
French speakers (the Norman elite) ate the meat, using French words: boeuf → beef, porc → pork, mouton → mutton, veau → veal


The echo of power in today’s menu

Same animals, two languages, two social classes
The animal word stayed English; the meat word came from French
Prestige: French commence, reside, purchase beside English begin, live, buy


What about chicken? It’s the English word for both bird and meat. The French-derived word poultry names the category.





England and Normandy




Geraghty, p. 167. Click once to reveal the right column. Chicken is an exception to the pattern: chicken (Old English cicen) stays for both, and poultry (from French poulet, poule) names the group. Ask what other pairs students can think of (“pig/pork” ~ Māori poaka, see the Pacific examples slide). The pattern is a tendency, not a law; mention that eating habits differ and nuance exists (for example, “lamb” is Old English and the meat is also “lamb”). Body-part pairs for extension: eye/ocular, heart/cardiac, mouth/oral, nose/nasal, tooth/dental.
Map: England and Normandy across the Channel. Point to Normandy (bottom right) as where the new ruling class came from, and to the Channel as the short distance between the two. If you want a caption, add the map’s source and date; save the image as images/norman-conquest-map.jpg.

title: Borrowing: How Languages Take Words
text:
Needed vs. Intimate Borrowing


Needed (“cultural”) borrowing
A new thing or idea arrives; the language needs a name for it.

Latin: bishop, monk
Hawaiian: kelekalama ‘telegram’, lekiō ‘radio’
English: ʻukulele, hula


Intimate borrowing
Constant close contact and bilingualism. Even sounds, particles, and constructions are borrowed. Over time the languages can converge, or the weaker one can be lost.

Norse: they, egg, take


What’s borrowed depends on how close the contact is: nouns first; then verbs and adjectives; grammatical particles (prepositions, conjunctions, affixes) last.

Counterexample: Germany ruled Western Samoa 1890-1914 with business interests since the 1850s. Samoan borrowed only a handful of rarely-used German words. Why?


Geraghty, p. 170 (Lynch 2004:197-199: little close contact, so little borrowing; Lynch’s chapter title, ‘Don’t take my word for it,’ plays on Schütz’s). Answer: contact alone is no guarantee; what matters is the closeness of contact and bilingualism. Ask students to compare with Palauan and Japanese schooling (Oct 6): schooling created close contact and many loans.
ANSWER to the Samoa/Germany question: contact alone does not produce borrowing. Germany had commercial interests from the 1850s and ruled 1890-1914, but there was little close, everyday contact and little bilingualism in German among Samoans, so only a handful of rarely used words were borrowed. Closeness of contact and bilingualism, not just political control, predict how much is borrowed. Contrast with Norse in English (intimate) and Japanese schooling in Palau (many loans).

title: Borrowing: How Languages Take Words
text:
After Cook: Build or Borrow?
New things arrived and needed names. At first, Hawaiians mostly built words:







Strategy
Hawaiian example




Compound
ʻīlio-nui ‘horse’ (‘dog-big’), later lio; mokulele ‘airplane’ (‘ship-fly’)


Semantic expansion
pūpū ‘shell’ → ‘buttons’; moku ‘island’ → ‘ship’; uila ‘lightning’ → ‘electricity’


Borrowing
pipi ‘cattle’ (beef), ʻaila ‘oil’, kākini ‘stocking’ (before 1810); kelekalama, kelepona, lekiō



Hawaiians were among the most literate people in the world then, avid readers of newspapers.

Discuss: Why might speakers prefer a compound like mokulele over borrowing the English word?


Geraghty, pp. 168-169. The chapter says borrowings in the 20th and 21st centuries are discussed in the language planning section (see “Who Decides?” below). Answer: transparency, fits the sound system, signals identity; but borrowing is faster.
ANSWER: building words from existing parts is transparent (mokulele explains itself), fits Hawaiian sounds without changing them, keeps the language’s own resources in use, and signals identity; borrowing is faster and easier when many new things arrive at once. Hawaiians did both.

Hawaiian borrowed English words in two periods. Compare the sets:



Before the missionaries
English

Pokekona

huelopoki
whaleboat

In pairs: (1) What vowel is added after a final consonant in each set? (2) What happens in clusters? (3) Who was in control of the form?

Geraghty, p. 171 (Schütz 1976:88, 1994:202). Before: the vowel added after a final consonant is usually /i/ or /e/ (with /u/ after the bilabials /m/ and /b/, as in kapu ‘tub’ and ukamu ‘oakum’); in huelopoki an /o/ breaks up a cluster. After: the missionaries decided /e/ goes between clustered consonants and /a/ goes after a final consonant. Exceptions: ʻapokolo ‘apostle’, ʻepikekolo ‘epistle’. Takeaway: early loans were shaped by Hawaiian speakers; later ones by missionaries, who wanted consistency and perhaps to exert authority. Pele ‘bell’ vs. pela ‘spell’ shows the two systems side by side.
ANSWERS: (1) Before the missionaries: a final vowel is added after a final consonant, usually /i/ or /e/ (kāpiki, lami, puke, pele, pine), sometimes /u/ after /m/ or /b/. After the missionaries: always /a/ after a final consonant (pela, kopa, hipa, Kenemaka). (2) Before: a vowel breaks up a cluster, e.g., /o/ in huelopoki. After: /e/ goes between clustered consonants (Pokekona, Kenemaka). (3) Before: Hawaiian speakers shaped the forms; after: the missionaries decided the pattern, to be consistent and probably to exert authority.

title: Borrowing: How Languages Take Words
section: “Take My Word for It”: Words Imposed
text:
“Take My Word for It”: Words Imposed
Missionaries (1820s on) taught religion and school subjects in Hawaiian, so they, not Hawaiian speakers, chose the new words. Schütz (1976): “Take my word for it.”


Built from Hawaiian

kāhikolu ‘trinity’ (‘one-three’)
alahou ‘resurrection’ (‘rise again’)
akua ‘god’ → the Christian God
keʻa ‘crossed wood’ → ‘cross’


Borrowed

hīmeni ‘hymn’, kāpaki ‘sabbath’, papakema ‘baptism’, ʻānela ‘angel’
“Eye borrowings” (from spelling, not sound): hīmeni; ʻeuanelio ‘gospel’ (Latin/Greek); ʻaeko ‘eagle’ and meli ‘honey’ (Greek); kinola ‘lyre’ and naheka ‘snake’ (Hebrew)



Discuss: Compare with Honiara last week: who decides which words and which languages count?


Geraghty, pp. 168 and 171. Eye borrowings are similar to the learned coinages from classical languages in English (television). Contrast with the earlier “Before the missionaries” loans, which Hawaiian speakers shaped. Tie to Jourdan & Angeli’s colonial hierarchy.
ANSWER to the Honiara question: in Honiara, English sat at the top of a colonial hierarchy and Pijin was called ‘broken English’; in Hawaiʻi, the missionaries decided which words the language would take. In both cases, people with institutional power (colonial authorities, missionaries, schools) decided what counted as a proper word or language, and speakers’ own preferences often came second. Differences: Hawaiian speakers had a very high literacy rate and still resisted some forms (the sounds /b d r s t/ never caught on).

The World Loanword Database (WOLD)
WOLD (Haspelmath & Tadmor 2009) is a free online database: word lists for 41 languages, each with 1,000-2,000 entries, written by experts. Every entry is coded for borrowing:



Code
Meaning




1
clearly borrowed


2
probably borrowed


3
perhaps borrowed


4
very little evidence for borrowing


5
no evidence for borrowing



Each loan lists its source word and donor language.
Austronesian languages in WOLD: Hawaiian, Takia (Papua New Guinea), Indonesian, Malagasy (Madagascar). Plus Ceq Wong, an Austroasiatic language of Malaysia, for contrast. We’ll practice on English.

Example row (Hawaiian): pipi · ‘the cattle’ · 1. clearly borrowed · source word beef (English)


Predict: What percent of English words do you think are clearly borrowed?


Live demo (see the next slide for the English demo): you can also show wold.clld.org/vocabulary/30 (Hawaiian). Show (1) the Borrowed status filter above the table (choose “1. clearly borrowed”), (2) the line “Showing 1 to 100 of 188 entries,” (3) the Meaning box for typing “cattle,” and (4) the language page wold.clld.org/language/30, where the Donor languoid column lists every loan by donor (230 entries). By default the Core list filter is set to True, which is what students will see. Question to ask the class: what do you think we’ll find? Sample prediction answers: more loans in nouns than verbs; mostly English as donor; more loans in technology and religion than in body parts. Four of the five lab languages are Austronesian (Hawaiian, Takia, Indonesian, Malagasy), which ties back to Week 2 (Blust); Ceq Wong (Austroasiatic, Malaysia) is the contrast, and its main donor, Malay, is itself Austronesian. Citation: Haspelmath, Martin and Uri Tadmor (eds.) 2009. World Loanword Database. Leipzig: Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology. wold.clld.org

title: Borrowing: How Languages Take Words
text:
Demo: English in WOLD (4 min)
Open wold.clld.org/vocabulary/13 (English). Set Borrowed status to 1. clearly borrowed.
Before we look, predict which of these English words are borrowed:


cattle · money · school · tea

All four are borrowed.

cattle ← Latin capitāle
money ← Anglo-Norman French
school ← Greek skholē
tea ← Min Chinese tiä


bread · mother · hand · eat are native (no evidence for borrowing).

Then: they, sky, egg ← Old Norse; tattoo ← Tahitian tātau. Which donor is biggest overall?


Live demo on English so no group’s language is spoiled. Steps to model for the class: (1) open the vocabulary page; (2) filter Borrowed status to “1. clearly borrowed” and read “Showing 1 to 100 of 585 entries” (of 1,515 core entries, 38.6%); (3) remove the filter to read the total; (4) type “cattle” in the Meaning box and read the row; (5) open the language page (wold.clld.org/language/13) and sort by donor. ANSWERS: cattle is from Latin capitāle (a surprise: the English word for the animal is itself a loan, while cow is native; this links to the cow/beef slides), money from Anglo-Norman French, school from Greek skholē (via Latin), tea from Min Chinese tiä. Native (coded 5): bread, mother, hand, eat, also cow, pig, sheep, chicken. Donors among clearly borrowed English words: Latin 263, French 61, Old Norse 43, Anglo-Norman 40, Greek 39, Late Latin 35. Norse examples from the chapter: they, sky, egg (all in WOLD). Tattoo ← Tahitian tātau is in WOLD as a loan. Note that the Meaning box searches WOLD’s meaning labels (e.g., “the cow”), not English words. Prediction answer for the previous slide: 38.6% of core entries are clearly borrowed (about 41% counting probable loans, as in Tadmor et al.).

ANSWERS / TALKING POINTS: Hawaiian 12.7% (English, plus Greek and Hebrew via missionary translation, Māori and others via the Lexicon Committee); Takia 23.1% (English, Tok Pisin, neighboring Bargam and Gedaged); Ceq Wong 33.6%, with about 95% of its loans from Malay (302 of 318); Indonesian 30.2% (Sanskrit, Dutch, Arabic, Javanese); Malagasy 12.5% (French 89, Malay 45, English 26, Bantu 17). Malagasy is the Austronesian language farthest west; WOLD lists “before the migrations to East Africa” as the contact situation for about 60 of its loans, a possible link to Week 2. Common pattern of the eight meanings: cattle, bread, money, school, and tea (introduced things) are borrowed nearly everywhere; mother, hand, and to eat (body, kin, basic verbs) mostly are not. title: Borrowing: How Languages Take Words
section: Language Nests and the Purist Turn
text:
Language Nests and the Purist Turn
Language planning = making and enforcing decisions on language use: education, writing systems, translators, and which words to use for new concepts.

In the 1800s, nearly all Pacific language planning was done by religious organizations
Hawaiian and Māori seemed headed for extinction ~50 years ago. Activists set up immersion preschools, language nests: kōhanga reo (Aotearoa, 1982) and pūnana leo (Hawaiʻi, 1983), which grew into schools and universities
Adults wanted to use the language at home and work, so they needed thousands of new words. The Polynesian Languages Forum (1991) coordinated this
Most activists wanted to distance the language from colonial languages: avoid loans as much as possible, build words by compounding and expansion

Computer: kamepiula (loan) or lolouila (lolo ‘brain’ + uila ‘electricity’)? Māori: rorohiko (roro ‘brain’ + hiko ‘spark’).

Debate: Is a “purist” policy good for a small language, when borrowing is a natural process?


Geraghty, pp. 173-174 (section 11); also see Schütz (1994:361-377) for Hawaiian and Holmes (2001), Harlow (2004) for Aotearoa. Verified in your uploads: Māmaka Kaiao lists lolouila (‘computer’, lolo + uila) alongside kamepiula, and Harlow’s chapter in Tent & Geraghty (2004) lists Māori rorohiko (‘computer’, roro ‘brain’ + hiko ‘spark, electricity’). DISCUSSION POINTS (no single answer): for purism: identity, distance from colonialism, transparency (lolouila explains itself), and learnable vocabulary for children in immersion schools. Against purism: borrowing is natural, speeds up coining, and keeps the language connected to everyday life of speakers who also use English. Next slide: the Hawaiian Lexicon Committee’s own guidelines show a practical middle path that does both.

title: Borrowing: How Languages Take Words
section: How Does a Committee Make a Word?
text:
How Does a Committee Make a Word?
The Hawaiian Lexicon Committee (founded 1987; kūpuna and native speakers from the start) meets 4-6 times a year. Every word must be approved at two meetings. Their dictionary, Māmaka Kaiao, records ten strategies:







Strategy
Example




Describe the concept in Hawaiian words
uila mahu pele ‘geothermal electricity’ (‘electricity-steam-volcano’)


Combine words
poelele ‘satellite’ (poe ‘buoy’ + lele ‘fly’); hamulau ‘herbivore’ (hamu ‘to chew’ + lau ‘leaf’)


Shorten and combine
ikehu ‘energy’ (ika ‘strength’ + ehu ‘lively’)


Add affixes
kalaianiau ‘climatology’ (kalai- ‘study of’ + aniau ‘climate’)


Extend an old word
haumia ‘pollution’ (old word ‘defiled, unclean’); hoʻoili ‘download’ (hoʻo- ‘cause’ + ili ‘transfer’; also ‘transplant’)


Borrow from another Polynesian language
pounamu ‘jade’ (Māori); makahiʻo ‘explore’ (maka ‘eye’ + Tahitian hiʻo ‘look’)


Hawaiianize a foreign word
naelona ‘nylon’; kaimine ‘saimin’ (Japanese); kokeiʻa ‘prairie dog’ (Ute); ʻōmā ‘lobster’ (French homard)




Discuss: The committee builds first but still borrows. Is that purism? What would you call it?


From the English introduction to Māmaka Kaiao (Hawaiian Lexicon Committee; 2003 edition, with the vocabulary created 1987-2000; ʻAha Pūnana Leo and Hale Kuamoʻo). The introduction lists ten guidelines; the table above gives seven. Others: make minor changes to an existing word (adding a kahakō), record words native speakers already use, and use reduplication (ulialia ‘coincidence’). Also in the book: Pūnaewele Puni Honua is the World Wide Web; uea makika (‘mosquito wire’) is a window screen. ANSWER / TALKING POINT: it is a pragmatic mix, not strict purism. The committee prefers Hawaiian resources, then other Polynesian languages, and only then Hawaiianizes non-Polynesian words, and the book itself uses kamepiula in an example sentence. This is the “build or borrow” choice from earlier, made by a community committee instead of missionaries (“Take my word for it”). The component glosses on the table: poelele (‘flying buoy’), hamulau (hamu + lau), kalaianiau (kalai- + aniau), haumia and hoʻoili (existing words with extended meanings) are from the dictionary entries in Māmaka Kaiao; ika ‘strength’, ehu ‘lively’, hamu ‘to chew’, and ili ‘transfer’ are from general Hawaiian knowledge, so check them against Pukui and Elbert before class. WOLD’s Hawaiian list includes many of these committee words as loans (the source is “Kōmike Huaʻōlelo 2003”), e.g., puolo ‘music’ from Māori puoro, and the Lexicon Committee’s Ute loans. Whether you call it purism is a matter of degree; students will have different views.

title: Borrowing: How Languages Take Words
text:
Putting It Together







Question
Answer from today




What is borrowing?
Sounds, words, endings, structures, meanings copied from another language; not code-switching


Why borrow?
Needed (new things) or intimate (close contact); also prestige (“unnecessary”)


What are the alternatives?
Compounding, semantic expansion, calques


What happens to loans?
Sound adaptation, semantic shift, reanalysis


Hawaiian history
Early builds, speaker-shaped loans, missionary-imposed forms, Hawaiian words that travel


Why linguists care
Etymological borrowing can disguise loans as inherited words


What gets borrowed?
Nouns > verbs/adjectives > function words; introduced things (WOLD data); body and kin words mostly not


Who decides?
Missionaries, communities, language planners: borrow or build?




Exit ticket (3 min): Pick one loanword from today (or one you use). What does it tell us about the relationship between the two languages, and how was it adapted?


Collect or use as the next Journal prompt. Terms that could appear on Quiz #4: borrowing, loanword, calque, code-switching, semantic expansion, compounding, semantic shift, reanalysis, etymological borrowing, intimate vs. cultural borrowing.
SAMPLE EXIT-TICKET ANSWERS: (a) pipi (Hawaiian) from English beef: shows cattle were introduced through contact with English speakers (Cook, Vancouver); adapted by changing /b f/ to /p p/ and adding a final vowel; later extended from meat to animal. (b) Kula ‘school’: a missionary-era loan; the vowel /a/ was added after the final consonant, showing the missionaries’ influence. (c) Pork in English: French-derived, showing French-speaking elites ate the meat. Accept any loan with a reasonable claim about the contact and a sound or meaning change.

title: The Origins of Hawaiian Pidgin
text:
Today’s Plan

What’s in the name “Pidgin”? Is it a pidgin or a creole?
A timeline: from first contact to a new language
Who shaped Pidgin’s grammar?
Pidgin’s vocabulary
Attitudes and Pidgin today
New research: Pidgin and Hawaiʻi English, schools, and UH
Looking ahead to Tuesday

title: The Origins of Hawaiian Pidgin
text:
“Pidgin”: One Word, Two Meanings


In Hawaiʻi

“Pidgin” is spoken by an estimated 600,000 people in Hawaiʻi, and by an unknown number of former residents on the mainland
Short for “Pidgin English”, the name English speakers gave it. They saw it as a simplified or “broken” English
Most of its vocabulary comes from English, but it is a separate language


In linguistics

A pidgin is a new language that develops when speakers of different languages need to communicate but share no common language
Used in limited circumstances, learned as a second language
When it gains native speakers and a full range of uses, it becomes a creole



So: Pidgin in Hawaiʻi is, linguistically, a creole. Other names: Hawaiʻi Creole English (HCE), Hawaiʻi English Creole, Hawaiʻi Creole.


Sakoda & Siegel, pp. 150-151. The word “pidgin” is thought to come from the Chinese pronunciation of business. This slide ties directly to Tuesday’s definitions (Meyerhoff): pidgin = restricted domains, no native speakers; creole = everyday use, children acquire it from birth. Don’t spend long here; the activity right after makes the distinction concrete.

title: The Origins of Hawaiian Pidgin
text:
Activity: Pidgin or Creole? (3 min)
In pairs. For each situation, decide: pidgin or creole? Be ready to explain.

Plantation workers from China, Portugal, and Japan use words from the overseers’ language to talk with each other at work
Parents speak the language with their babies at home. Those children use it with classmates, and it becomes their first language
The language is used only for giving orders and trade. No one speaks it at home
It is used for jokes, arguments, family talk, and school playground talk
It has a community of native speakers and a full range of functions, but people still call it “broken English”


Answers: 1 pidgin; 2 creole; 3 pidgin; 4 creole; 5 creole. The last one is the point of the day: linguists distinguish what a language is from what people say about it. Sakoda & Siegel define a pidgin as used in limited circumstances, learned as a second language; a creole as a language that developed from a pidgin and now has a full range of functions, a complex grammar, and native speakers.

title: The Origins of Hawaiian Pidgin
section: Pidgin Is One of Many Creoles
text:
Pidgin Is One of Many Creoles







Lexifier
Examples




English
Pidgin (Hawaiʻi), Jamaican Creole (Patwa), Gullah (South Carolina and Georgia coast), Guyanese Creole, Kriol (northern Australia), Krio (West Africa)


French
Louisiana, Haiti and other Caribbean islands, Mauritius and other Indian Ocean islands


Portuguese
Cape Verde, Guinea-Bissau, India, Malaysia


Other
Creoles with Arabic, Malay, and Ngbandi as lexifier




An estimated 41.7 million people speak creole languages
All have very different grammars from their lexifiers and from each other


Discuss: Jamaican Creole is used in reggae lyrics. Where have you seen or heard Pidgin used in music, books, or media?


Sakoda & Siegel, p. 151. Connect to Tuesday’s Melanesian creoles (Bislama, Tok Pisin, Pijin): same process, different lexifier history and substrate languages. Optionally add a world map of creoles here if you have one.

title: The Origins of Hawaiian Pidgin
text:
First Contact (before the plantations)

Polynesians settled the islands between about 200 and 400 AD; Captain Cook arrived in 1778 (native population estimated at 200,000 to 1,000,000)
Contact grew with the fur trade (1790-1810), sandalwood, and whaling. By 1848, only about 88,000 Hawaiians remained, mostly because of introduced disease
Traders and whalers learned some Hawaiian, and Hawaiians learned some English. No real pidgin yet, but features of other English pidgins were used
Still in Pidgin today: plenty (‘a lot’), by and by (future), no before a word to make it negative, and got/get (‘have’)


Callback (Oct 8): The chapter gives about 200-400 AD for settlement. Does that match the dates we saw for Hawaiʻi on Oct 8? Why might they differ?


Sakoda & Siegel, p. 152. Check this against the settlement dates on your Oct 8 slides; the chapter (2003) takes one position in a debate that has continued since, so newer estimates may be later. Features appear in Hawaiian sailors’ speech in Dana’s Two Years Before the Mast (1840), as discussed by Roberts (1998). Hana ‘work’ and pau ‘finished’ survive in pau hana.

title: The Origins of Hawaiian Pidgin
text:
The Plantations Bring the World
The first sugar plantation opened in 1835. Laborers came from:







Group
When and how many




China (mostly Cantonese speakers)
~2,000 (1852-76); more than 37,000 (1877-97)


Pacific Islands
~2,450 (1877-87): most from Kiribati, at least 550 from Vanuatu, others from Rotuma, New Ireland, Bougainville, Santa Cruz


Portugal (Madeira and Azores)
10,000+ (1878-87); 13,000 more (1906-13)


Japan
Began 1884; over 200,000 by 1924


Philippines
Began 1907; over 100,000 by 1930


Others
Korea (7,843), Puerto Rico (5,203), Russia (~3,000), Spain (~2,000), Germany (1,052), Norway and others (615)




Discuss: Imagine a plantation work crew: Chinese, Portuguese, Hawaiian, and Kiribati laborers. How would they talk to each other?


Sakoda & Siegel, p. 153. Point out the Vanuatu connection: some of the same Pacific Islanders who ended up on Queensland plantations (Bislama’s origin) were also recruited to Hawaiʻi. Callback to last Tuesday: Meyerhoff says Hawaiʻi’s plantation pidgin survived for demographic and social-psychological reasons, because it became a marker of local identity.

title: The Origins of Hawaiian Pidgin
section: The First Pidgin Was Hawaiian, Not English
text:
The First Pidgin Was Hawaiian, Not English

In the early plantation era, Hawaiians still ruled their islands. Hawaiian was the language of government and of education for non-European children, so it became the language used to run the plantations
Many white overseers and Chinese laborers never learned it fully. A new form emerged with words mostly from Hawaiian, but different pronunciation, meanings, and structure. When Portuguese laborers arrived in the 1870s, it consolidated
So the first real pidgin in Hawaiʻi was Pidgin Hawaiian

How Pidgin Hawaiian differed from Hawaiian:

Dropped the ʻokina: piʻi mai became pi mai, meaning ‘come’ (in Hawaiian: ‘climb in this direction’)
Changed meanings: hapai ‘bring’ (from ‘carry’), makana ‘give’ (from ‘gift’)
Changed forms: hana hana ‘work’, nuinui ‘many’
Borrowed: pihi ‘fish’ (English fish), kaukau ‘food, eat’ (Chinese Pidgin English chow chow)


Sakoda & Siegel, p. 153. Callback to last Tuesday: Meyerhoff said pidgin Hawaiian faded as English took over, and Hawaiʻi’s pidgin kept going. This slide shows the sequence: Pidgin Hawaiian first, then Pidgin English. Don’t read every example; choose two or three.

title: The Origins of Hawaiian Pidgin
text:
Activity: Decode Pidgin Hawaiian (5 min)
An immigrant’s testimony in a criminal court case, 1892:

Kela lio oe hele hauhau lela palani wau ma ka ponei. literally: that horse you go eat that bran I in the last-night

In pairs:

Translate it into natural English. (The court heard: Your horse went to eat my bran last night.)
Compare with Hawaiian: Ua hele kou lio e ʻai i kaʻu palani i ka pō nei. What is missing in the pidgin? (Hint: ua)
How is possession shown in each? (‘horse you’ vs. ‘your horse’)
Which word order is more like English?


Example from Sakoda & Siegel, p. 153 (quoting Roberts 1995:41). Answers: (2) the pidgin lacks ua (marks completed events); (3) the pidgin puts the possessor after the thing possessed (lio oe ‘horse you’, palani wau ‘bran I’), whereas Hawaiian puts the possessive word before (kou lio, kaʻu palani); (4) the pidgin order, ‘horse your went’, differs from both Hawaiian (‘went your horse’) and English. Good moment to tie to Tuesday’s simplification and “function words dropped” from the pidgin Māori activity.

title: The Origins of Hawaiian Pidgin
text:
The Shift to English

1875 Reciprocity Treaty with the US: free trade and more Americans. Hawaiians were fewer than 50,000 by 1878
1878 to 1888: English-medium schools increased dramatically, Hawaiian-medium schools declined
Chinese and Portuguese families arrived (earlier, laborers were mostly single men), so more children were exposed to English in public schools
English gradually replaced Hawaiian on the plantations, and an English-lexified pidgin began to develop. At first, a mixture of Pidgin Hawaiian and English words:


Oe no tumach holoholo, hausu stop, mama nana. ‘You no too-much travel-around, house stop, mother look.’


New features: too much (‘a lot’ or ‘very’), stop (‘stay, live at’), me for ‘I’


Sakoda & Siegel, pp. 154-155. Quick optional prompt: which words in the example are Hawaiian (holoholo, nana) and which English (hausu, stop, mama)? Also include pilikia in the second example (Roberts 1993). Hawaiian words came into early Pidgin English, especially plantation words: hana hana, hapai ko ‘load cane’, hanawai ‘irrigate’, hoe-hana ‘hoe’. The chapter notes the language changed from the dominance of Hawaiian to English starting in 1875.

title: The Origins of Hawaiian Pidgin
text:
Pidgin English Becomes Established

Late 19th century: people started saying things in similar ways and a new structure emerged. Hawai’i Pidgin English (HPE) was established as a new auxiliary language
Early 1900s: HPE spread in mixed urban areas and public schools (most standard-English-speaking European children attended private schools)
Locally born Japanese children learned HPE from classmates; children learned it from school-age siblings and used it as a second language at home
But still learned as a second language, so speakers’ first languages shaped how they spoke it (e.g., Chinese speakers’ hully for ‘hurry’, dropped final sounds, allee for ‘all’)


Discuss: Which of Tuesday’s three clues for a pidgin (stable norms, restricted domains, variation from first languages) does HPE show? Which one is changing?


Sakoda & Siegel, pp. 155-156. The chapter’s example is a 1937 play (Bond) in which two older Chinese men saw wood: features like l for r (hully, licee), dropped final sounds (goo’, ligh’), -ee endings (allee, licee), and allee same ‘like’ and got at the end of a sentence, do not survive in modern Pidgin. Features that do survive: pake, no mo’, no can, kaukau, bymby pau, um for ‘him, her, it, them’, wahine. Use the optional play-sorting slide if you have time.

title: The Origins of Hawaiian Pidgin
text:
From Pidgin to Creole

Around 1900, the second generation of locally born Chinese and Portuguese appeared. Most parents were bilingual in their language and HPE, and many used HPE as their primary language
Parents spoke to newborns in HPE instead of Cantonese or Portuguese. Many Part-Hawaiian children also learned HPE as a first language, since many interethnic marriages used HPE at home
Now spoken as a first language, HPE was technically no longer a pidgin: Hawaiʻi Creole, modern Pidgin, began to emerge
Most linguists agree Pidgin was established as a distinct language between 1905 and 1920. Between 1920 and 1930, locally born children of immigrants equaled foreign born, and Pidgin became the language of the majority of Hawaiʻi’s population


Discuss: Compare with Bislama (Tuesday). What’s the same, and what’s different?


Sakoda & Siegel, p. 157. Link to Meyerhoff pp. 147-148: urbanization, intermarriage, children acquiring the language from birth. Differences: no institutional recognition as a national language; in Hawaiʻi, the creole emerged inside a context of English-medium schools and immigrant labor, with no single indigenous lingua franca. Bislama was named the national language after independence partly because it was neutral. HCE has never been recognized officially.

title: The Origins of Hawaiian Pidgin
text:
What Did the Creole Add?
Modern Pidgin has less variation in pronunciation than the earlier pidgin, and new grammar:







New in the creole
Example




never for a past event that did not happen
I never do like that.


stay for continuing action
I stay working my house.


for meaning ‘to’
We are ready for play ball.



(Examples from a 1921 Hawaii Educational Review article that listed these as “incorrect” usage.)

Discuss: The 1921 article called these “incorrect.” Why do linguists disagree?


Sakoda & Siegel, pp. 157-158. The 1921 article also listed old pidgin features: I stop Honolulu, I no got pencil, Him blow my head, What for you talk like that?, I too much like that one, Suppose rain, I no can go, He look all same chicken. Many still survive. Key point: the chapter explicitly says linguists would not agree that structures in Pidgin or any other language are “incorrect” just because they differ from standard English. Tie to Jourdan & Angeli’s colonial hierarchy (Tuesday): “broken English” has the same logic.

title: The Origins of Hawaiian Pidgin
text:
Three Substrate Languages
Hawaiian

Word order: Nui ka hale (‘big the house’) → Pidgin: Big, da house; Cute, da baby
Exclamations: Auwē, ka nani! (‘oh the pretty!’) → Oh, da pretty!

Cantonese

yáuh means both ‘have’ and ‘there is/are’ → Pidgin get: They get three sons. / Get one student he very bright.

Portuguese

para ‘for’ → fo/for: Charles is da man fo do ’um.
estar (location, state, progressive, result) → stay: Da book stay on top da table. Da water stay cold. John stay writing one letter. Da house stay pau already.


Sakoda & Siegel, pp. 159-160. Use this as the central “substrate” slide, tying to Tuesday: the languages speakers already know shape the creole’s grammar (compare Bislama’s inclusive/exclusive ‘we’ from Vanuatu languages). Also: the pronunciation of Pidgin has similarities to Hawaiian, Cantonese, and Portuguese, especially in vowel sounds and intonation in questions, but this has not been studied in detail.

title: The Origins of Hawaiian Pidgin
text:
Activity: Match the Source (4 min)
In pairs. Which language does each Pidgin feature seem to come from? (Hawaiian, Cantonese, or Portuguese)

Get three sons. and Get one student he very bright. (one word for ‘have’ and ‘there is’)
Da house stay pau already. (one word for several kinds of ‘be’)
Big, da house. (adjective before the noun phrase)
***Charles is da man fo do ‘um.*** (’for’ where English says ‘to’)
Oh, da pretty!


Then: pick one feature and explain how you know it’s not from English.


Answers: 1 Cantonese (yáuh); 2 Portuguese (estar); 3 Hawaiian (Nui ka hale); 4 Portuguese (para); 5 Hawaiian (Auwē, ka nani!). English contrast: English uses have vs. there is; be with different forms; ‘the house is big’; ‘to’ with infinitives; ‘how pretty!’. This is a great live demonstration of the comparative method idea: the same sort of reasoning we used for cognates.

title: The Origins of Hawaiian Pidgin
text:
Why Portuguese More Than Japanese?
Japanese was the largest immigrant group, yet it influenced the grammar less. Why?

Timing: the first large Japanese immigration came in 1888, by which time Hawaiians, Chinese, and Portuguese had pretty well fixed the form of the pidgin (Reinecke 1969)
Locally born matter: it was locally born children who acquired the pidgin as a first language. Portuguese locally born equaled foreign born by 1900; Chinese just before 1920; Japanese later in the 1920s
Portuguese were the largest locally born immigrant group in 1896 (over half) and the largest immigrant group in schools (1881-1905, over 20% from 1890-1905)
Plantation power: Portuguese held many skilled and luna (‘foreman’) positions, three times as many as any other group
Language shift: the Portuguese were the first group to shift from their traditional language to Pidgin


But Japanese left a mark: about 40 words, translations like chicken skin ‘goose bumps’, discourse particles (yeah, no at the end of a sentence), and the structure of narratives.


Sakoda & Siegel, pp. 160-161. Discussion prompt: which factor matters most: numbers, timing, children, schools, or power? What does this say about how languages change? (Answer: the number of speakers is not enough; who is positioned to acquire the language as a child, and when, matters.) Sources cited: Roberts (2000), Siegel (2000), Masuda (2000), Reinecke (1969).

title: The Origins of Hawaiian Pidgin
text:
Words from Everywhere
Most Pidgin words come from English, but many have changed meaning or form, and many come from other languages:


English words, new meanings

pear ‘pear, avocado’
pipe ‘pipe, faucet’
shame ‘shame, shy’
off ‘turn off’ (off the light)
broke ‘broken, torn’

New compounds

talk story, stink eye, chicken skin, bolohead, bulai (bull + lie)


From other languages

Hawaiian (100+): akamai, kokua, ono, pau, pilikia, ʻohana, keiki
Japanese (~40): bento, shoyu, musubi, mochi, obake
Portuguese: malassada
Chinese: char siu, lihing mui
Filipino: adobo, bagoong
Korean: kimchee
Samoan: lavalava



Sakoda & Siegel, pp. 161-164. Other blended forms: haolefied, onolicious, hulihuli chicken, kalua pig, poi dog, chawan cut, daikon legs, buta kaukau. Point: Pidgin is not “English with errors”: it has its own meanings and word-building.

title: The Origins of Hawaiian Pidgin
section: Activity: Whose Word Is It? (4 min)
text:
Activity: Whose Word Is It? (4 min)
In pairs. Sort these words by their source language: Hawaiian, Japanese, Chinese, Portuguese, Filipino, Korean, Samoan, or English (changed).
akamai · bento · malassada · kimchee · pau · pilikia · kaukau · lavalava · adobo · char siu · shoyu · bulai

Then: write a sentence in Pidgin that uses at least three of these words, and tell your partner what it means.


Answers: akamai Hawaiian; bento Japanese; malassada Portuguese; kimchee Korean; pau Hawaiian; pilikia Hawaiian; kaukau from Chinese Pidgin English chow chow; lavalava Samoan; adobo Filipino; char siu Chinese; shoyu Japanese; bulai English-derived compound (bull + lie). Remember that students who speak Pidgin are the experts: invite them to share a surprising origin.

title: The Origins of Hawaiian Pidgin
section: A Badge of Identity, and a Target
text:
A Badge of Identity, and a Target

Pidgin has mostly been the informal language of families and friends, an important badge of local identity
Attitudes have always been ambivalent: important to local culture, but also called corrupted or “broken” English and seen as an obstacle to learning standard English, the language of schools, government, and big business
1987: the Hawaiʻi Board of Education tried to adopt a policy allowing only standard English in schools. Parents, teachers, university faculty, and community groups reacted strongly; the policy was seen as discriminatory, and as an attack on Pidgin and local culture
Similar debates followed (1999, 2002), as some officials and members of the public blamed Pidgin for poor reading and writing test results


Compare with Tuesday (Honiara): Pijin was also called “broken English” and ranked below English. What do the two situations have in common? What’s different?


Sakoda & Siegel, p. 164 (see Sato 1989, 1991). The chapter was published in 2003, so all “recent” events are about 20+ years old. Consider adding any current developments you want to mention (for example, current school policies, UH initiatives, or media). Connect to Jourdan & Angeli: social vs. linguistic legitimacy; hierarchical ideology; “Pijin spoelem English” vs. the claim that Pidgin hurts students’ standard English. Hawaiʻi’s difference: backlash from the community in 1987 was strong and public.

title: The Origins of Hawaiian Pidgin
text:
Pidgin Gains New Domains

Da Pidgin Coup (since 1998): a group mainly from UH Mānoa that meets regularly on linguistic, social, and educational issues about Pidgin. Their position paper, “Pidgin and Education,” gave research-backed information to officials and teachers
Print: Pidgin to da Max (1981) and its sequel sold more than 200,000 copies. Bamboo Ridge Press (1978) spurred local writing. Authors include Eric Chock, Lisa Kanae, Darrell Lum, Milton Murayama, Ed Sakamoto, Gary Pak, Lee Tonouchi, and Lois-Ann Yamanaka
Bible: Da Jesus Book (2000) sold over 11,000 copies in its first year


Discuss: Tuesday’s definitions: a pidgin has restricted domains; a creole is used in a full range of functions. How does expanding into writing and publishing fit this picture?


Sakoda & Siegel, p. 164. These are the chapter’s examples of Pidgin’s expanding domains as of 2003. If you want a current example, add one here (a recent book, show, or social media creator) to show that expansion has continued; I did not verify anything newer than the chapter.

title: The Origins of Hawaiian Pidgin
text:
Heavy, Light, and In Between
Pidgin is not one fixed way of speaking:







Term
What it means




Basilect (“heavy” or “strong” Pidgin)
Very different from English


Mesolects
Varieties in between; where most speakers are


Acrolect (“lighter” Pidgin)
Close to standard English




Many speakers switch between heavier and lighter Pidgin depending on who they’re talking to, what they’re talking about, the setting, and the level of formality. Many are fully bilingual in Pidgin and standard English
A common belief: Pidgin is gradually becoming more like English. But the variation seems to have existed from the earliest days, and the wish to project a local identity will likely keep Pidgin distinct
There is no general agreement about what counts as Pidgin: for some, only the heavy basilect; for others, a local accent and some local words


Discuss: Where would you draw the line? Can someone “speak Pidgin” with an accent and a few words?


Sakoda & Siegel, p. 165. Shifting between heavier and lighter Pidgin is movement along a continuum. Connect to Tuesday’s Meyerhoff on dialect differences arising as children regularize variation.

title: The Origins of Hawaiian Pidgin
text:
Activity: The 1987 Hearing (12 min)
Groups of 5-6. Roles: Board of Education member, parent, classroom teacher, UH linguist, local author or poet, student
The Board proposes a policy: only standard English in schools. Each group holds a short hearing:

Prepare (4 min): In your role, write 2-3 points. Use evidence from today (attitudes, variation, expanding domains, Jourdan & Angeli, Tuesday’s Vanuatu readings)
Hearing (6 min): Each role speaks for 45 seconds. Then the Board member summarizes and proposes a compromise policy
Share (2 min): Each group announces its compromise


Think about: Is the policy about Pidgin, or about standard English? Can schools support both?


Role-play based on the 1987 Board of Education proposal described by Sakoda & Siegel (p. 164). Make sure students know it’s a simulation of a real historical controversy. Check in with students who speak Pidgin: they are the experts, but don’t put them on the spot. Possible compromise policies: standard English as the target for formal writing while allowing Pidgin in speaking and as a bridge; teacher training about language variation (the Da Pidgin Coup’s approach). Alternative if time is short: run it as a 5-minute pair discussion.

title: The Origins of Hawaiian Pidgin
text:
English Standard Schools



Public schools were English-medium by law (1896), yet in the 1920s white families newly arrived from the US lobbied for separate “English Standard” schools
Admission was by an oral English test. Children who failed, mostly Pidgin-speaking children of plantation workers, went to the regular schools
Phased out in the 1940s; the last class graduated in 1960
At UH Mānoa, teacher trainees were tested on English in the 1920s, and in 1943 freshmen who didn’t improve in required speech courses could be dismissed (speech courses stayed required into the 1970s)


Two effects

Pidgin-speaking kids stayed together, which kept Pidgin alive
Pidgin got tied to lesser education, and English to the white elite


Discuss: How is this different from what happened to Hawaiian in schools after 1896?



Higgins (2021), “Promoting Pidgin at UH Mānoa,” Ch. 10, pp. 1-3 (history section). Higgins quotes a 1920 Bureau of Education statement that white parents feared their children “would be outnumbered by the orientals,” so the issue was race and class as much as language. The link to Drager (2012): by the 1910s, Roberts (2004) finds English already associated with haole identity and Pidgin with being “local.” Discussion answer: Hawaiian-medium schools were closed down (nearly gone by 1896) and Hawaiian stopped being passed on in many homes; with Pidgin, schools kept Pidgin-speaking children together and, ironically, helped maintain it. Compare Tuesday’s colonial hierarchy in Honiara (English on top).

title: The Origins of Hawaiian Pidgin
text:
Pidgin vs. Hawaiʻi English
Most people in Hawaiʻi speak Pidgin, Hawaiʻi English, or both, and switch between them. Drager (2012) treats them as two languages on a continuum. Same lexifier, different grammar:








Feature
Pidgin
Hawaiʻi English




Past
I wen go. (wen, or ben on Kauaʻi; optional if the time is clear)
I went.


Negation
We no eat dea. / We neva eat dea. (neva for past)
We don’t / didn’t eat there.


Complements
I wen go downtown fo eat lunch. (fo ← Portuguese para)
…to eat lunch.


“Be”
Da stew stei nice. (stei ← Portuguese estar; adds surprise)
The stew is nice.


Adjective first
Cute, da baby. (like Hawaiian ʻOno ka iʻa)
The baby is cute.




In one study of fifth graders on Hawaiʻi Island, many had under 70% comprehension when listening to their non-dominant variety
Discourse particles (yeah, eh, no) show up in both, likely from Japanese


Discuss: Why do people say “broken English” about Pidgin, when the grammar here is so regular?


Drager (2012), “Pidgin and Hawaiʻi English: An overview,” pp. 61-73, sections 6-7; Reynolds (1999) for the comprehension study. Also Sakoda & Siegel (2012) in the Mouton World Atlas of Variation in English: preverbal markers for tense and aspect (stay habitual and progressive, bin and go for anterior and future) are typical of creoles; the use of stay shows the Portuguese substrate (estar). Drager’s footnote: linguists write “pidgin” for the contact variety and “Pidgin” for the creole. Mufwene’s “feature pool”: speakers draw from both. Connect to Tuesday: lexifier vs. substrate, and to the heavy-to-light slide (basilect, mesolect, acrolect). Hawaiʻi English also has its own history: Drager notes two meteorologists who sued the National Weather Service in 1987 over hiring on the basis of how they “sounded” (they were speaking Hawaiʻi English, not Pidgin).

title: The Origins of Hawaiian Pidgin
text:
Mapping Pidgin on Oʻahu
Drager & Grama (2014) gave people a blank map of Oʻahu and asked where people talk differently. They never mentioned Pidgin or English.


What they found

Maps followed the old moku (districts)
Waiʻanae and Waimānalo marked as Pidgin; Hawaiʻi Kai and Kāhala marked as English
Town: many languages (e.g., Ilocano, Samoan, Chinese)
Many maps added ethnicity, though the task asked only about language
Where Pidgin was named in “English” areas, it was a lighter Pidgin


Why it matters

People hold detailed, shared beliefs about place, ethnicity, and language
These beliefs are ideologies, like Jourdan & Angeli’s in Honiara


Activity (3 min): Sketch Oʻahu (or your home island). Where do you think people talk differently? What label would you give?



Drager & Grama (2014), Dialectologia 12, pp. 23-51. First perceptual dialectology study within Hawaiʻi. Table 2: 19 of 22 respondents who mentioned Waiʻanae labeled it Pidgin (86.4%). The study found that people believe language, ethnicity, and region are linked. Earlier work by Preston (1982, 1986) used a map of the US, where Hawaiʻi was just one spot labeled “Pidgin.” Caution for class: these are beliefs about speech, not measurements of speech; the authors note that further work should compare beliefs with actual variation. Invite students from other islands to share. Keep the discussion non-judgmental about neighborhoods.

title: The Origins of Hawaiian Pidgin
text:
Putting It Together







Stage
What happened




Contact (1778-1830s)
Traders and whalers; features of English pidgins; no real pidgin yet


Pidgin Hawaiian (1830s-1870s)
Hawaiian dominant; plantations; words mostly Hawaiian


Pidgin English (1875-1900s)
English replaces Hawaiian; new auxiliary language; too much, stop, no


Creole (1905-1930)
Locally born children acquire it as a first language; new grammar (never, stay, for)


1920s-1960
English Standard schools sort children by spoken English


Today
Marker of local identity; expanding into print; taught and studied at UH; debated in schools




Exit ticket (3 min): Pidgin is a creole, but many people still call it “broken English.” Using one piece of evidence from today, explain why linguists say that’s wrong.


Dates from Sakoda & Siegel, pp. 152-157. Collect exit tickets or use as the next Journal prompt. Possible strongest evidence: substrate-based grammar (get, stay, for), the new grammar added by children (never, stay, for), regular patterns; native speakers; full range of functions.

Activity: Make It Easier (4 min)

Then, pairs: rewrite “I was supposed to meet him at the farmers market, but the bus was running late.” for a visitor who knows only basic English. What did you change?

Examples (1)-(2) are from Meyerhoff, p. 141. The (b) versions use everyday vocabulary and joined or juxtaposed simple clauses. title: Pidgins and Creoles
text:
Two Strategies: Simplification and Accommodation


Simplification

Plainer, non-technical vocabulary, avoiding dialect words
Combining simple sentences with and/but (coordination), or just placing them side by side (parataxis)
That’s not my teddy. His tummy is too shiny…


Accommodation

Speakers converge on a compromise between their ways of speaking
It shows up in speed, volume, vowels, sentence structure, and vocabulary
You may have noticed that you slow down when talking with someone who talks slowly



In radical contact, simplification and accommodation can produce new, distinct varieties: pidgins and creoles.


Meyerhoff, pp. 141-142. The chapter’s points: yelling does not help; simplification and accommodation together explain how pidgins emerge. Callback to last Thursday’s “Same Language, or Different?” slide: Tupaia and Cook’s crew probably relied on simplified, gesture-assisted talk.

title: Pidgins and Creoles
section: Why Didn’t Traders Learn the Local Languages?
text:
Why Didn’t Traders Learn the Local Languages?
Meyerhoff (citing Le Page & Tabouret-Keller 1985): three conditions for learning a language well








Condition
Missionaries
Traders and plantation managers




Motivation
Strong (to convert people)
Profit, not communication


Long exposure
Years living in the community
Brief encounters, long gaps


Regular use
Full participation with speakers
Little chance to practice




Many incomers also assumed their culture was superior and were reluctant to learn or accommodate
Later, as colonizers increased, locals were expected to accommodate, picking up basic competence in the traders’ language


Meyerhoff, p. 143. The table condenses her argument; do not present it as her table. Emphasize the power dimension: pidgins are not “failed attempts to learn English,” they are stable solutions to restricted communication needs. This sets up the colonial ideology material (Honiara) where “broken English” is the stock insult.

title: Pidgins and Creoles
text:
What Makes Something a Pidgin?
Meyerhoff gives three clues, using pidgin Māori as the example:

Relatively stable norms, even for a short time. You could rely on the same features from one trader to the next, months apart
Restricted domains: needed for business or trade, not for everyday family and community life
Variation tied to speakers’ first languages: everyone has another dominant language, which can colour things like word order

Pidgin: a contact variety used by adults for restricted purposes, with no native speakers.
Creole: what happens when speakers use it in a wider range of everyday domains (jokes, arguments, chores, flirting) and children acquire it from birth. Many linguists treat that point, children acquiring a pidgin as a first language, as the moment it becomes a creole.

Discuss: Which of these three clues would be hardest to see in the historical record? Why?


Meyerhoff, pp. 143-144, for the three clues. Pidgin/creole wording follows Meyerhoff, pp. 145-148: expanded domains plus children’s acquisition; in practice, she notes, adult expansion and children’s acquisition usually go hand in hand, so it is rarely possible to separate them. Matches the Oct 1 slide on creolization. Bickerton (1981) in the chapter: word-order variation reflecting speakers’ L1s (Japanese SOV, Filipino languages VSO, Chinese/English SVO).

title: Pidgins and Creoles
text:
Activity: Read the Pidgin (5 min)
Early 19th-century pidgin Māori (recorded by Savage in 1807):

Tungata nue nue kikie man big big eat ‘That man has plenty to eat’

Compare Standard Māori: He nui ngā kai a tēnā tangata.
In pairs:

What do you notice about the pidgin version? Hint: look for function words (determiners, possessives)
What does nue nue (‘big big’) do? Where have we seen doubling in the Pacific?
Why would a trader find the pidgin version easier than the standard one?


Example (3) in Meyerhoff, p. 144 (quoting Clark 1990:103, Savage 1807). Features missing from the pidgin: determiners and possessive markers (tēnā, a). Reduplication (‘big big’) is a common intensifier across Pacific languages, including Melanesian Pidgin (we’ll see lukluk in the Bislama text). Link to last Thursday: Tupaia and Cook; Drechsel (2014) suggests it’s better to treat this as a general Maritime Polynesian Pidgin, not separate Tahitian and Māori pidgins.

title: Pidgins and Creoles
text:
What Does “Simple” Mean?
Pidgins are often called simple. Meyerhoff says to be careful:

Simple for adult second-language learners. Languages with complex sounds or grammar (Russian, tonal Cantonese) are just as easy for children to acquire. Pidgins are used by adults for specific purposes, so children aren’t learning them as first languages
Fewer productive rules. Fewer overt function words and often no subordinate clauses: speakers use parataxis (chains of bare clauses)


The food that is for our dinner is on the table.
becomes: The food is on the table; it is for our dinner.


Simplifying one thing complicates another: more ambiguity, more variation between speakers, and a processing cost for decoding differences


Discuss: Is “simple” the same as “broken”?


Meyerhoff, p. 145 (Trudgill 2011 for the point about children and complexity). Good moment to prepare the “broken English” attitude material coming up: pidgins are not failed English; they are stable systems that are simple in specific respects, for specific speakers.

title: Pidgins and Creoles
text:
Trading Languages Without Europeans
Meyerhoff: trading pidgins existed with no European input. Documented examples include trading varieties of Drehu (New Caledonia), Pohnpeian (FSM), Fijian and Hindi (Fiji), Aleut, Chinook, Vietnamese, Yimas, and Tetun.
One famous case: Hiri Motu (Papua New Guinea)

The hiri was the annual trading voyage of the Motu people, about 200 miles across the Gulf of Papua
Hiri Motu was the form of Motu they used on those trips


Discuss: What do trading varieties like Hiri Motu share with pidgin Māori, even though one has no European input?


Meyerhoff, pp. 144-145 (Hiri Motu citing Dutton and Brown 1977). Drechsel (2014) on a Maritime Polynesian Pidgin. Answer to the discussion: restricted domain (trade), stable norms, speakers with other first languages.

title: Pidgins and Creoles
section: Why Did Some Plantation Pidgins Survive?
text:
Why Did Some Plantation Pidgins Survive?








Pidgin
What happened
Meyerhoff’s explanation




Melanesian Pidgin (Tok Pisin, Pijin, Bislama)
Taken home from Australian plantations; stabilized and developed
Extensive linguistic diversity in Melanesia


Samoan plantations
Introduced, but did not last
Samoa is essentially monolingual


Hawai’i
Survived
Demographic and social-psychological reasons: a marker of “local” identity


Chinese Pidgin English, Unserdeutsch (pidgin German in colonial PNG)
Did not last
not discussed




Pidgin Māori and pidgin Hawaiian faded as locals shifted to pidginized English. In Hawai’i, that pidgin gained enough demographic support to continue; in Aotearoa, shift to English was much more substantial


Discuss: Samoa lacked a language need that Melanesia had. What does that tell us about why pidgins survive?


Meyerhoff, pp. 144-145. The plantation pidgin used in Australia drew on a vehicular language further south in Australia, then was carried back to Melanesia. Connects to Day 11 (Samoa 1 indigenous language vs. Vanuatu ~100) and to Thursday’s Hawai’i reading. Last row’s explanation is not given in the chapter; say so if asked.

text:
Three Sister Languages



Tok Pisin (Papua New Guinea), Bislama (Vanuatu), Pijin (Solomon Islands)
Linguists treat them as varieties of one Melanesian Pidgin. English is the lexifier (the source of most of the vocabulary), but grammar and word-building come from Melanesian languages
Their history is tied to the plantation pidgin of Australia, which drew on a vehicular language further south. Islanders recruited to work Queensland sugarcane plantations in the second half of the 19th century brought it home, where it stabilized and developed
In the Solomons, it spread through mission stations (the South Sea Evangelical Church on Malaita) and plantations where language diversity was high





Sources: Meyerhoff, p. 145 (plantation pidgin, lexifier); Jourdan & Angeli (2014), p. 268, drawing on Keesing (1988, 1990) (Queensland, mission stations). Day 11 and Oct 1 already covered the 19th-century plantation/trade origin and urbanization-creolization; the new details here are Queensland and the mission-station route. Schütz’s Tok Pisin 3-5 million speakers figure was in the Oct 1 slides.

title: Pidgins and Creoles
text:
Activity: Read the Bislama (5 min)
From the Bislama summary of a 2025 article on Vanuatu school policy (Tarihehe & Willans):

Atikol ya hem i ripot blong wan stadi we i lukluk hao nao oli putum tugeta venakula edukesen polisi blong Vanuatu long ol selected skul long West blong Ambae.

Read it aloud with a partner. Then:

Sound out each word. Which ones can you guess from English?
lukluk and putum tugeta: what are they built from?
How would you translate it? Then check the authors’ English version on the next slide


From the Summary in Bislama in Tarihehe & Willans (2025), Te Reo 68(3): 71. Likely glosses (mine, not from the chapter): atikol = article; hem i ripot = it reports; blong wan stadi = of a study (‘belong one study’); lukluk = look, examine (reduplication); putum tugeta = put together; venakula = vernacular; edukesen polisi = education policy; long = in/at; skul = school. Great moment to point out that Bislama is the written “everyday” language of the article summary: even an academic text can be in Bislama. Be careful: Bislama spelling is still variable and not fully standardized.

title: Pidgins and Creoles
text:
Authors’ English Version

This article reports on a study that investigated the implementation of Vanuatu’s vernacular education policy in selected schools on West Ambae.


Notice how much of the Bislama vocabulary is English-derived (stadi, polisi, skul), but the grammar and word-building are not English: an i marker before the verb, reduplication (lukluk), and -um on transitive verbs (putum)
Question: is Bislama “broken English”? Hold that thought for the next section


English text from the paper’s abstract (Tarihehe & Willans 2025). The grammatical points (agreement marker i, reduplication, transitive -um) are illustrated in Meyerhoff’s examples (5)-(7), pp. 146-147, which the next section uses. This sets up the “broken English” ideology slide in the next section.

title: Pidgins and Creoles
text:
How a Pidgin Expands
Meyerhoff’s case study: Vanuatu. The plantation pidgin brought home from Australia did not disappear. Why?

Work migration: a growing plantation economy within Vanuatu brought people with different first languages together
Social value: the pidgin seems to have carried connotations of worldliness and experience abroad
From instrumental to affective: adults moved beyond getting tasks done to expressing feelings and relationships. Swearing appears early: blari ‘bloody’ is attested from the early 20th century
Urbanization and intermarriage: in Port Vila and Luganville, Bislama became the default town language, sometimes even on the islands in marriages across language groups
National recognition: after independence, Bislama was named the national language partly because it was neutral, belonging to no single group


Discuss: Which of these five reasons also applies to Hawai’i Pidgin? Which doesn’t?


Meyerhoff, pp. 146-148. “Instrumental vs. affective” functions: even task language is affective (if you like me you’ll do business with me again). Bridges the Oct 1 “From Pidgin to Mother Tongue” slide, which covered urbanization. New here: the instrumental-to-affective expansion and the neutrality of Bislama as a national language.

title: Pidgins and Creoles
section: Where Bislama Gets Its Grammar: The Substrate
text:
Where Bislama Gets Its Grammar: The Substrate
The speakers’ first languages form the substrate (sub ‘beneath’ + stratum ‘layer’). Bislama has features that don’t occur in English but match the Eastern Oceanic languages of Vanuatu:







Feature
Bislama example




Inclusive vs. exclusive ‘we’
yumi ‘you and me’ vs. mifala ‘us but not you’


Transitive suffix -em/-im/-um
singaot ‘call’ vs. singaotem ‘call (someone)’


Reduplication for intensity or number
katkat-em bamboo ‘cut lots of bamboo’


‘Say’ to introduce a clause
Mifala i talem se Jeni i stap ‘We said that Jenny was here’




Activity (3 min, pairs): Does English have an inclusive/exclusive ‘we’? How do you ask “Shall we go?” if the other person is not coming?


Meyerhoff, pp. 146-147, examples (4)-(7). Tie back to Tuesday last week (Marshallese had two words for ‘we’, inclusive and exclusive: Bender). The point is that Bislama is not “English with the endings dropped”: its grammar is built from the substrate. Example glosses from the chapter: AGR = agreement marker i; TR = transitive suffix.

title: Pidgins and Creoles
text:
What Did Children Add?

Children who acquire a pidgin as a first language regularize variation and add features, including dialect differences among groups of speakers
Evidence from Bislama on Malo Island: children made a clearer split between third-person pronouns and all others. First- and second-person subject pronouns are kept more consistently than in adult speech; both groups often drop third-person pronouns
But: there is remarkably little data on children’s creole acquisition, especially for ages 7-15, so it is hard to say any one feature was introduced by children


Discuss: Meyerhoff argues adults and children both shape creoles. Why might the old story that “children invent creoles” be too simple?


Meyerhoff, pp. 147-148 (Figure 1). Do not overinterpret the pronoun figure; the chapter itself says the data are limited. Key claim: in practice adult expansion and children’s acquisition go hand in hand.

title: Pidgins and Creoles
text:
Honiara: A Young City
Jourdan & Angeli (2014) study the language ideologies around Pijin in Honiara, capital of Solomon Islands.

Honiara was created after WWII on Guadalcanal, on the site of a US army base. By 2014, about 65,000 people, more than half under 25
71 languages, plus English (official language, language of school) and Pijin (de facto national language, no official status)
Two generations of native Pijin speakers. Some children, especially from mixed marriages, don’t know their parents’ ancestral languages; Pijin is their mother tongue
In schools, literacy is acquired in English only, and written public communication is in English


Jourdan & Angeli (2014), pp. 267-269. 64,609 is the estimate they report; 36,334 under 25. Pijin has been codified by Christian associations for Bible translation, and a full dictionary exists since 2002 (Jourdan 2002), but few people are literate in it. Honiara connects directly to the Oct 1 “From Pidgin to Mother Tongue” slide (urbanization → creolization): this is an up-close case study.

title: Pidgins and Creoles
text:
Four Language Ideologies
Language ideologies = culturally shaped attitudes about what language is, how it should be used, who should use it, and what it’s worth. Jourdan & Angeli find four layers in Honiara:








Ideology
When
Core idea




Reciprocal multilingualism
Precolonial
All vernaculars are equal; neighbors learn each other’s languages; multilingual people earn prestige


Hierarchical multilingualism
Colonial
English on top; vernaculars called “dialects”; Pijin called “broken English”


Linguistic pragmatism
Throughout, now reshaped
Learn the language that gets you somewhere. Today, that’s English as a global language


Linguistic nationalism
Recent
Local languages should be recognized and used in school; one nation, one people, one language




Jourdan & Angeli (2014), pp. 270-276. Key framing: ideologies accumulate and compete, “like old shells filled with new meanings.” Reciprocal multilingualism links back to François (Oct 1): no village outranks another, everyone learns neighbors’ languages. Their distinction: perceptions (what people say) vs. ideologies (the underlying reasoning, often unconscious). Nationalism is described as influenced by European “one nation, one language” ideas; mention purism.

title: Pidgins and Creoles
text:
The Colonial Hierarchy
Colonial language ideology rested on three assumptions:

“True” languages are written: so unwritten vernaculars (and Pijin) don’t count
Purism: change and mixing are “decay”; real languages are “natural” and unchanging
Language shows civilization: English was the language of progress; local languages were “backward”

Result: colonials called vernaculars “dialects”, called Pijin “broken English,” and expected it to be a temporary stage on the way to “proper” English.

Discuss: Think back to language vs. dialect earlier in the course. Who gets to decide which one a variety is? Where have we seen the label used as a ranking?


Jourdan & Angeli (2014), pp. 271-272, citing Calvet (1979), Keesing (1990), Crowley (2000) on Vanuatu (once English, a written language, entered, local people were labeled illiterate and many devalued their own languages). Note the irony Jourdan & Angeli point out: from a long-term historical view, all languages (English most obviously) were born from contact. Callback: in Chuukic, the 70% ‘language limit’ is a technical, not a social, criterion.

title: Pidgins and Creoles
text:
Two Stock Phrases
Still part of “common sense” in the Solomons today (and in schools):


Pijin hem broken English nomoa
‘Pijin is just broken English’
Based on the belief that Pijin came from a failed attempt to learn English. Many people say Pijin has “no grammar.” Interviewers found that putting “Pijin” and “grammar” in the same sentence made people laugh

Pijin spoelem English
‘Pijin ruins English’
Based on the idea of interference: that you should speak either Pijin or “proper” English. People are not supposed to be bilingual in both


Discuss: What evidence from today (pidgin Māori, the Bislama text) shows that Pijin and its relatives do have internal structure?


Jourdan & Angeli (2014), pp. 272-273. Interview data: 14 middle-aged professionals and civil servants, 27 Solomon students (19-25) at USP in Honiara and Suva, plus focus groups. The older elite were schooled where speaking Pijin was forbidden and often punished. Young educated Honiarans rarely challenge the stock phrase, even those who grew up with Pijin as a mother tongue. Make sure to name the point: “broken English” misunderstands what pidgins are (stable systems with their own norms).

title: Pidgins and Creoles
text:
What Young Honiarans Say Now
The hierarchy remains, but its meaning has shifted:

English is no longer justified as “the language of civilization.” Students say it’s the language of the global community: university, jobs, international communication
In practice, English is a gatekeeper: all national exams are in English, and university degrees must be completed abroad
Nationalism: some argue Pijin is part of national identity and that urban children who speak only Pijin need recognition; others do not want Pijin used as the national or school language
Jourdan & Angeli’s puzzle: Pijin has social legitimacy (it’s everyone’s city language) but not linguistic legitimacy


Discuss: Can a language be socially legitimate but not linguistically legitimate? Where might this describe Pidgin in Hawai’i?


Jourdan & Angeli (2014), pp. 274-277. This is a bridge to Thursday’s Hawai’i Creole reading and to Discussion Post #5 if the prompt allows. Students’ idea of English as a gatekeeper links back to Lynch’s ‘metropolitan’ language and to Oct 1’s two-school-system slide. The students interviewed are mostly second-language speakers of Pijin per the examples; the speakers named in the paper’s quotes are not identified further, so don’t treat them as real individuals in class.

title: Pidgins and Creoles
text:
Activity: Which Ideology? (6 min)
In groups of 3-4. For each statement, decide which of the four ideologies it reflects (reciprocal multilingualism, hierarchical, pragmatism, nationalism). Some may fit more than one: argue your case.

“If you want a government job, you need English. That’s just how it is.”
“Visitors should learn at least a few words of Pijin. It’s polite.”
“Pijin isn’t a real language. It doesn’t even have a grammar.”
“Our school should teach in our own language. That’s who we are.”
“My cousin speaks four languages, and everyone respects her for it.”
“The old people punished us for speaking Pijin at school, but now I use it with my friends.”

Then: write a statement about Hawai’i you’ve heard, and decide which ideology it fits.

Original statements written for class, paraphrasing the ideologies in Jourdan & Angeli (2014); they are not quotes from the paper. Suggested answers: 1 pragmatism; 2 reciprocal multilingualism (Learning the local language is a mark of respect: p. 271); 3 hierarchical/colonial (the ‘no grammar’ belief); 4 nationalism; 5 reciprocal multilingualism; 6 hierarchical (older elite) + shift toward pragmatism. Discussion: statements often mix ideologies, which is exactly the authors’ point: ideologies accumulate and speakers use them strategically.

title: Pidgins and Creoles
section: Which Language Do People Understand Best?
text:
Which Language Do People Understand Best?
Schneider, Gooskens, Kapelle & Antón-Méndez (2025): an intelligibility study in Vanuatu

Question: do well-educated ni-Vanuatu understand spoken English as well as spoken Bislama, especially in professional settings (courts, business, education)?
Background: about 89% of written government communication is in English (7% Bislama, 4% French), yet 86% of ni-Vanuatu respondents in one survey call speaking Bislama very important to national identity
Test: 58 students at USP in Port Vila, compared with 55 Australian university students, who heard English varieties and Bislama sentences and answered comprehension questions
Findings: ni-Vanuatu have much more exposure to Bislama, prefer it, feel more confident about it, and responded more accurately to Bislama sentences than to English ones


Schneider et al. (2025), Te Reo 68(3): 20-60. Percentages for government communication are from the 2019 Bulu report (Office of the Ombudsman) as cited in the paper; the 86% figure is from Mudaliar et al. (2024) as cited. The paper emphasizes the legal system, where English continues to dominate (a ni-Vanuatu legal scholar argued for using Bislama in the Supreme Court), and recommends modest strategies for giving Bislama greater prominence.

title: Pidgins and Creoles
text:
Discussion: What’s at Stake?

Discuss (3 min): If even well-educated ni-Vanuatu understand Bislama better than English, what does it mean that court judgments, tender documents, and government notices are written in English? Who benefits, and who is left out?


Bislama is the language most people speak. English is the language of official writing
This is the same gap Jourdan & Angeli describe in Honiara: social legitimacy without official legitimacy


Connect to Lynch’s ‘metropolitan language’ (Ch. 7) and the Oct 1 Vanuatu two-parallel-school systems slide. Let students notice the equity argument: speakers of the dominant variety enjoy socio-economic advantages (the paper cites Labov 1966 and Bernstein 1971 for the general point).

title: Pidgins and Creoles
section: Learning in Which Language? West Ambae
text:
Learning in Which Language? West Ambae
Tarihehe & Willans (2025) tested children in two primary schools on West Ambae (Vanuatu), in Years 1 and 4, in three languages: Nduindui (the local vernacular), Bislama, and English


What they found

Strongest ability in Nduindui; minimal English; Bislama mixed
Little difference between Year 1 and Year 4: little new language acquisition in the first three years of school
In class, Nduindui carried spoken interaction, but English was the only language on the board


What people said

Teachers and communities strongly support the vernacular policy
By Year 4 the vernacular was seen as something to fall back on when English was hard, not part of a growing plurilingual repertoire



Tarihehe & Willans (2025), Te Reo 68(3): 71-105. Trilingual picture-based language assessment; classroom observation; teacher interviews; community hunguhungu (talking sessions). Conclusion in the abstract: Nduindui was the most logical language for the principal medium of instruction in Year 1, and students were no more ready to use English for this purpose by Year 4. Ties back to the Oct 1 slide on Vanuatu’s school system (Bislama or vernacular in Years 1-2; English or French from Year 3).

title: Pidgins and Creoles
section: Activity: You Run the Ministry (10 min)
text:
Activity: You Run the Ministry (10 min)
Groups of 4. You are advisers to Vanuatu’s education ministry. Decide the language of instruction for Years 1-3 and Years 4-6.
Use at least three pieces of evidence from today or earlier:

Schneider et al.: understanding of Bislama vs. English
Tarihehe & Willans: Nduindui, Bislama, and English in classrooms
Jourdan & Angeli: the four ideologies (who will object, and why?)
Lynch / Oct 1: Vanuatu has ~100 languages, so which vernacular?

Report out (1 min each): your recommendation, your strongest piece of evidence, and the strongest objection you expect.

Open-ended policy task. Good tension: with ~100 indigenous languages, vernacular education is hard to scale; Bislama is widely understood but has less prestige and fewer written resources; English and French are gatekeepers for secondary school and exams (and parallel school systems from the condominium). Possible outcomes: Bislama as a bridging language in lower grades; vernaculars in selected communities; explicit English instruction as a subject. Whatever groups pick, push on trade-offs and who is excluded.

title: Pidgins and Creoles
text:
Putting It Together








Stage
What it is
Example




Contact
Speakers of different languages need to talk
Traders, labour trade, plantations


Pidgin
Stable, restricted-use contact variety used by adults; no native speakers
Pidgin Māori; Hiri Motu; early Melanesian Pidgin


Creole
Used in everyday life and acquired by children from birth
Bislama (national language), urban Pijin, Tok Pisin


Ideology
Attitudes shape status, school, and law
“Broken English”; English as gatekeeper



Meyerhoff’s closing point: in many places, local creoles are still seen as “bad” examples of English (or French or Spanish). People fail to appreciate how systematic and complex their structure is, and fail to recognize their importance as symbols of local and personal identity.

Exit ticket (3 min): Pick one claim about pidgins or creoles that you believed before today. Did anything today challenge it? What’s the evidence?
