title: Pidgins and Creoles
text:
Activity: Build a Pidgin (20 min)
Groups of 4: two Tavu speakers and two Dezi speakers. These are invented languages: each pair gets a card with 20 words and a word order. Goal: trade (fish, yams, pigs, water for knives, cloth, shells).








Round
Time
What you do




1. No shared language
4 min
Trade using only your own language and gestures. No English. Note what happens


2. Build the pidgin
6 min
Create a trade language of at most 20 words. Choose words (Tavu, Dezi, or new) and a word order


3. Next day
4 min
One Tavu and one Dezi speaker move to another group. Trade using only your pidgin. What breaks?



Use the Pidgin Sheet: for each concept, write the word and its source.

Materials: Build_a_Pidgin_Handout.docx (Tavu card, Dezi card, Pidgin Sheet, facilitator notes). Print one Tavu card and one Dezi card per pair. The two languages are built to differ in two ways that matter: word order (Tavu verb-final, Dezi verb-first) and ‘we’ (Tavu has an inclusive/exclusive distinction, Dezi has one word), mirroring Bislama’s substrate features (Meyerhoff, p. 146). Timing: set up 2 min, rounds 4 + 6 + 4, then move to the debrief. Circulate in Round 2 and listen for: whose words win, whether the group chooses one word order, whether they keep kita/kami, and what they drop. Round 3 tests stability (Meyerhoff’s first clue for a pidgin). If the room is small, make groups of 3 (one Tavu pair-speaker doubling up) or run two rounds only.

title: Pidgins and Creoles
text:
Build a Pidgin: Debrief
Compare notes across groups (5 min). Put these on the board:







Question
Link to Meyerhoff




Whose words did you use, Tavu’s or Dezi’s? Why?
Lexifier and power: who has the advantage in contact


Which word order did you pick? Did anyone use both?
Substrate influence; variation tied to speakers’ first languages


Did you keep two words for ‘we’?
A feature that survives in Bislama (yumi / mifala)


What did you leave out (endings, little words)?
Simplification; fewer function words; parataxis


What broke in Round 3?
Stability: norms must hold across people and time


Could this pidgin handle a family argument or a joke?
Restricted domains




Discuss: What would have to happen for your pidgin to become a creole?


Ties each result to Meyerhoff pp. 143-148: stable norms, restricted domains, substrate influence, simplification and parataxis, and the creole step (everyday use and children acquiring it from birth). Likely patterns: groups pick one language’s words for most nouns (often whichever pair spoke first or loudest), drop the inclusive/exclusive ‘we’ (sometimes keep it), and settle on verb-first or verb-last with variation across groups. Round 3 almost always reveals mismatches in word choice between groups, which is the point: stability takes time and shared use. Answer to the discussion question: wider domains of use (jokes, arguments, household talk) and children acquiring it as a first language.

title: Multilingualism & Language Diversity (cont.)
text:
Vanuatu, Revisited


Michael asked: how can one small island group have languages so different that neighboring islands can’t understand each other?
Dyllan asked: when a language is only spoken by a few hundred people and isn’t being passed to kids, what happens next — and does losing the language mean losing parts of the culture?

Discuss: What would it take for a language with a few hundred speakers to survive another generation?





Tie back to Tuesday’s three factors (time, separation, social structure) — Vanuatu is the extreme case of all three stacking together.
Dyllan’s question, updated: Crowley (2000) famously argued Bislama posed no real threat to Vanuatu’s indigenous languages. A 2025 review (Lavender Forsyth) challenges that — 2020 census data show only 14% of Vanuatu’s population now speaks an indigenous language as their first language, and in rural areas as many as 1 in 5 people aged 4-20 have Bislama, not an indigenous language, as their first language. That’s the mechanism behind Dyllan’s question: kids growing up with Bislama at home instead of the local language breaks the chain of transmission. Don’t over-explain this — just flag it, since full language endangerment is covered in a later unit.

title: Multilingualism & Language Diversity (cont.)
text:
Why So Many Languages?


Linguist Alexandre François has spent decades documenting this exact puzzle in northern Vanuatu (the Torres and Banks Islands).

17 languages, 9,400 people — all descended from one ancestor language, 3,000 years of divergence
Isolation alone doesn’t explain it — people there are constantly in contact: trading, intermarrying, visiting
Language as identity marker: communities deliberately keep their speech different from close, friendly neighbors — François calls this language’s “emblematic function”
Egalitarian multilingualism: no village outranks another, so no variety becomes “the” prestige language — everyone just learns their neighbors’ languages instead





François (2012)



Discuss: If isolation alone doesn’t explain Vanuatu’s diversity, what does this suggest about places that are very isolated but still only have one language?



Direct answer to Michael’s and Dyllan’s questions, grounded in François (2011, 2012). Key reframe: diversity isn’t an accident of geography, it’s maintained on purpose. Also sets up Dyllan’s endangerment question — the same egalitarian multilingualism that sustains tiny languages today is exactly what’s eroding under colonial-era disruption and modern schooling (mention briefly, don’t dive deep — save for later unit on endangerment).

title: Multilingualism & Language Diversity (cont.)
section: Zooming Out: Is This Just Vanuatu?
text:
Zooming Out: Is This Just Vanuatu?

Not unique to the Pacific: linguists call this pattern “small-scale” or “egalitarian” multilingualism — the same setup (many small languages, no prestige hierarchy, everyone multilingual) is documented in West Africa, the Amazon, and northern Australia too (Lüpke 2016; Pakendorf, Dobrushina & Khanina 2021)
A bigger claim: linguist Nicholas Evans (2018) argues this may be close to the ancestral human condition — that language itself likely evolved in multilingual small-scale societies, not isolated monolingual ones
If he’s right, multilingualism isn’t the exception that needs explaining — monolingual nation-states are the historically recent, unusual case


Discuss: If small-scale multilingualism was the human norm for most of history, why does monolingualism feel like the “default” to so many people today?


~5 min. Good note to end the Vanuatu thread on: reframes the whole unit. Monolingualism isn’t neutral/natural — it’s a product of nation-state language policy, mass schooling, and standardization, which is a much more recent development than multilingual small-scale societies. Don’t need to resolve the discuss prompt — just let it sit before moving to Kale’s question.

title: Multilingualism & Language Diversity (cont.)
text:
Vanuatu’s Other Language Split


Jinghao’s question: the reading mentions ni-Vanuatu learn English or French depending on their school — how is that distributed? Do families choose, or is it based on where they live? Is there debate about it?

Vanuatu was jointly ruled by Britain and France until 1980 — a colonial “condominium” — and kept two entirely separate, parallel school systems at independence rather than merging them
Schools register as English-medium or French-medium, not mixed; children usually attend whichever is available locally, often tied to earlier missionary history in that area
Years 1-2: Bislama or the local vernacular; English or French phased in by Year 3; Years 3-13: instruction entirely in English or French
The split isn’t a strict geographic English-region/French-region boundary — it’s institutional, school by school, a direct legacy of the colonial system surviving 45+ years after independence




Discuss: Why might a newly independent country choose to keep two parallel colonial-language school systems rather than consolidating into one national language of instruction (English, French, or Bislama)?



Direct answer to Jinghao’s question. Good follow-up point if time: this is a different kind of “diversity” than the indigenous-language diversity from earlier slides — this one is purely a colonial-era institutional artifact, not organic. Worth distinguishing the two kinds of multilingualism for students.

title: Multilingualism & Language Diversity (cont.)
text:
Language and Local Knowledge
Kale’s connection: in BOT 444 (Ethnoecology), Kale has studied how Indigenous and Local Knowledge (ILK) develops over generations through a community’s relationship with its environment — and noticed this tracks closely with how Lynch describes language diverging through geographic and social separation.
Kale’s question: could neighboring language groups in Melanesia have different names, classifications, or knowledge systems for the same plants and animals?

Discuss: If language and ecological knowledge both diverge through isolation, which one do you think usually changes first?


This is a strong interdisciplinary connection — worth explicitly praising in class. If no one has a confident answer to the discuss prompt, that’s fine; the point is raising the possibility that linguistic diversity and biocultural diversity are entangled, not resolving it today.

title: Multilingualism & Language Diversity (cont.)
text:
Kale’s Question, Globally
David Harmon (1996) compared the countries with the most endemic languages (found nowhere else) to the countries with the most endemic vertebrate species (mammals, reptiles, birds, amphibians found nowhere else).

64% overlap between the top 25 countries on each list
Papua New Guinea ranks #1 for endemic languages (847) and in the top 10 for endemic vertebrate species
His explanation: the same conditions — rugged terrain, isolation, small-scale societies — that let species diverge into new forms also let languages diverge into new forms. One doesn’t cause the other; both are downstream of the same isolation


Discuss: Harmon’s explanation is about geographic isolation producing both effects in parallel. How does this compare to François’s claim (from the Vanuatu slides) that language diversity is partly deliberate, not just a byproduct of isolation? Could both be true at once?


Answers Kale’s question at the macro/statistical level: diversity of language and diversity of species co-occur geographically, worldwide, not just impressionistically in Melanesia. Harmon (1996), Southwest Journal of Linguistics. Good moment to have students hold two explanations in tension rather than picking one — isolation-as-shared-cause (Harmon) vs. deliberate differentiation (François) aren’t mutually exclusive.

title: Multilingualism & Language Diversity (cont.)
text:
Example
A concrete case: the Kalam people of the Upper Kaironk Valley, Papua New Guinea highlands (~13,000 speakers).


Zoology (Bulmer 1967): Kalam classify cassowaries separately from all other birds — not by mistake, but because cassowaries occupy a unique role in Kalam thought and ritual. Their system also sorts animals by habitat (forest vs. garden vs. homestead; aerial vs. terrestrial vs. underground), not just by body shape the way Western biology does.


Botany (Gardner 2010): Kalam distinguish roughly 500 named plants — many finer-grained than Western scientific species, some grouping things Western botany splits apart.

Discuss: Bulmer titled his paper “Why is the cassowary not a bird?” What does it tell us that this is a real, serious research question?



This is the direct, concrete answer to Kale’s original question — yes, a documented Melanesian group has a classification system for plants/animals that diverges meaningfully from both Western science and (presumably) from neighboring groups, though a direct neighbor-to-neighbor comparison wasn’t found in this search. Emphasize: Kalam taxonomy isn’t “wrong” or “primitive” — it’s organized around different, equally coherent criteria (ritual significance, habitat, practical use) rather than evolutionary descent.

title: Multilingualism & Language Diversity (cont.)
section: This Research Is Happening Right Now
text:
This Research Is Happening Right Now
A 2024 PhD dissertation — from right here at UH Mānoa — documented exactly this kind of plant knowledge for the Abui people of Alor Island, eastern Indonesia (A.L. Blake, advised by Gary Holton). It’s a direct, current answer to Kale’s question about how a group actually classifies plants.


Names encode different kinds of knowledge, not just appearance:

al fiyaai “nettlespurge,” lit. “Islam candlenut” — two plants that look nothing alike, linked because both were burned for lamp oil; the name preserves history, not shape
fia beeka “fern bad” — marks a fern as inedible, in contrast to “good” (edible) ferns — classification by utility
kupai meeting “forest betel-vine” — classification by habitat


Metaphor drives the categories, often from the body or animals:

kaai hawet “Ziziphus,” lit. “dog its teeth” (thorns)
wata muur “pomelo,” lit. “coconut citrus” (fruit size)
katiki “Conyza,” lit. “loincloth broke” (shredded-looking leaves)


Discuss: Western botany classifies primarily by evolutionary descent. Abui plant names show at least five other organizing logics — history, utility, habitat, body-part metaphor, taxonomic prototype. Is any one of these more “correct” than the others?



This is the most direct, current answer to Kale’s actual question. Good closing move on the Kale thread: shows this isn’t settled 1960s-70s scholarship (Bulmer) — it’s live research, happening now, at Andy’s own institution, on a different island group from Vanuatu/PNG, reinforcing that this pattern isn’t one-off. The “metaphor hardening into taxonomy” point (alokai example) is worth dwelling on — it shows folk classification isn’t a fixed system handed down unchanged, it’s actively being renegotiated as new plants and new generations enter the picture.

title: Multilingualism & Language Diversity (cont.)
text:
From Pidgin to Mother Tongue
Francesca’s question: Bislama, Tok Pisin, and Pijin all started as simplified contact languages for 19th-century trade and plantation labor — how does a language like that become someone’s actual first language?

The short answer: urbanization, not a deliberate decision. As towns like Port Vila, Port Moresby, and Honiara grew, people from many different indigenous-language backgrounds ended up living side by side
With no single shared indigenous language in these mixed communities, the pidgin — already everyone’s common second language — became the only shared language of daily life
Adults kept making the pidgin more expressive through ordinary creative use, even before any child spoke it natively
Once children in these communities grew up hearing only the pidgin at home, it became their native language — this is creolization: pidgin → creole happens when a generation of kids acquires it as a first language
The scale today: Tok Pisin alone has an estimated 3-5 million speakers, many now native


Discuss: This is the same process (urbanization, a shared contact language taking over daily life) driving the Bislama/indigenous-language shift from earlier in class. Is a pidgin becoming a creole a loss, a gain, or both?


Direct answer to Francesca’s question, and a nice bridge back to Dyllan’s endangerment thread — same underlying mechanism (urbanization + a dominant contact language) creates new creole-speaking generations AND erodes smaller indigenous languages simultaneously. Worth being explicit that this is not a contradiction, it’s the same process viewed from two angles.

title: Multilingualism & Language Diversity (cont.)
text:
One Person, Several Languages
Linguists call it domain-based language choice (or, when it’s stable over time, diglossia): multilingual speakers don’t use their languages interchangeably — they assign specific languages to specific settings, like home, school, work, or religion.


Chloe’s post: growing up in Hawai’i with a Chinese family background, Chloe noticed she speaks differently depending on who she’s talking to — English at school, another language at home — and connected this to why multilingualism is so common across the Pacific.
Hanna’s post: a student from Ecuador who speaks four languages, Hanna noticed the exact triglossic pattern Lynch describes for Vanuatu (local language at home, Bislama in public, English/French at school) in her own life — German and Spanish with family, English for university, English and Spanish with roommates in Hawai’i.

Kiana’s question: multilingualism in Melanesia/Polynesia often develops out of necessity, not choice — does that change how it’s experienced? In Kiana’s own social circles, people react to multilingualism with excitement, suspicion, or by “dumbing down” their speech around less-fluent listeners. Do speakers in the Pacific relate to their own multilingualism the same way?

Discuss: Map your own languages (or registers, slang, codes) onto their domains — which goes with which setting? Then: does multilingualism by necessity feel different from multilingualism by choice?



~5-7 min. Leading with the concept (domain-based choice / diglossia) is what this slide was missing — Chloe and Hanna’s posts are both textbook illustrations of it, not just personal anecdotes. Don’t let it stay abstract — if the room is quiet, offer your own example first. Kiana’s question is good to leave genuinely open as the close of the discussion-posts section — it pushes students past treating multilingualism as self-evidently good, into examining their own assumptions.

Four Kinds of Pacific Languages







Category
Description




① Indigenous
Native to the country or territory — what most of this course has focused on so far.


② Metropolitan
The colonial or national language of government, education, and formal life — usually English, sometimes French, Spanish, or Indonesian.


③ Pidgin / Creole
Contact languages like Bislama, Tok Pisin, Pijin — covered in depth Thursday.


④ Immigrant
Languages brought by more recent arrivals. Lynch sets this aside in the chapter — keep it in mind for Fiji.




~4 min framing. New content from Ch.7 §2. Flag pidgin-creole is a quick callback only. End by flagging Fiji Hindi as a preview — technically “immigrant” by this framework, yet functions almost like a metropolitan language.

title: Why Is Melanesia So Linguistically Diverse?
text:
Vanuatu vs. Samoa


Team Vanuatu

~100 indigenous languages, ~250,000 people
Jointly ruled by England & France until 1980 — both English and French are official
Bislama spoken by ~95% of the population
Typical ni-Vanuatu speaks 3+ languages: local language at home, Bislama in town, English or French at school/work
Port Vila: ~85% of the country’s languages have some speakers there


Team Samoa

1 indigenous language: Samoan
Former German colony (to WWI), independent from New Zealand since 1962
Just two languages in daily use: Samoan and English
Samoan is the medium of instruction in primary school
English = formal/modern settings; Samoan = basically everywhere else



~3 min setup. Split the room in half: Team Vanuatu and Team Samoa. Each group gets their fact sheet and 5 minutes to script a “day in the life.”

Fijian — actually a dialect chain; eastern/western and northern/southern speakers don’t always understand each other. A standardized eastern variety is used officially.
Rotuman — spoken on Rotuma, part of Fiji but its own language, related to Fijian but distinct.
Fiji Hindi — brought by Indian indentured laborers in the late 1800s.

~60,000

Discussion: Fiji

Fiji has real internal diversity — the Fijian dialect chain plus Rotuman — that looks more like the Melanesian pattern.
But a standardized Fijian and English both function as unifying, public-life languages — more like the Polynesia/Micronesia pattern.
And then there’s Fiji Hindi — a whole additional layer neither pattern predicts, because it’s about 19th-century indentured labor migration, not indigenous settlement history.


Discuss: What does Fiji teach us about the limits of a two-category explanation?


~4 min discussion. Cold-call or pair-share.

title: Why Is Melanesia So Linguistically Diverse?
text:
The Telephone Tree

Four communities, one ancestor — split into 4 groups. Everyone starts with: “The octopus stole my sandwich at the market.”
Pass it down — telephone-style within each group, several rounds, no writing anything down.
A later split — split each of the 4 groups in half again, run one more short round within each half.
Compare all eight — write all 8 final versions on the board. Which resemble each other? Which drifted furthest?


~12-15 min. This models Lynch’s Figure 1 (branching diversification) experientially, no phonetics required.

title: Why Is Melanesia So Linguistically Diverse?
text:
Telephone Tree: Debrief

Notice: the two halves that split from the same group later usually still sound more alike than the more distantly split groups. That’s exactly the branching pattern behind real language families.



~50,000 yrs — settlement in parts of Melanesia (New Guinea region)

~3,000 yrs — oldest settlements in Polynesia/Micronesia

~1,000 yrs — since Hawaiʻi and New Zealand were first settled


~4 min debrief + bridge. More “rounds” = more drift = more languages.

title: Why Is Melanesia So Linguistically Diverse?
text:
Three Explanatory Factors


① Time
More generations = more drift (just modeled with Telephone Tree).

② Separation
Geographic AND social isolation. Surprise: the sea is often NOT a barrier — coastal communities across a strait can be more similar than communities on the same island.

③ Social Structure
Polynesian societies: large, hierarchical — holds one language together. Melanesian societies: small, egalitarian — harder to keep one language unified.


~5 min mini-lecture.

title: The Languages of Polynesia
section: Reading the Past Without Written Records
text:
Reading the Past Without Written Records
Schütz: looking back thousands of years for the origins of Polynesian languages, we find only the most durable clues.



Lapita pottery was first made in New Britain and Mussau around 1,400 BC, and its makers can be traced back another two thousand years to Taiwan
Languages ancestral to Polynesian were spoken during this long period of exchange, though no epics or chants mark the milestones
Researchers reconstruct earlier movements with archaeology, radiocarbon dating, DNA studies, and above all language — in complex relationship with people’s movements, which can cut off communication





Decorated Lapita pottery, Bourewa site, Fiji




Discuss: Why might language be the most important evidence for Polynesian origins, when we also have pottery, DNA, and radiocarbon dates?


Schütz, p. 97. The chapter notes that scholars’ estimates of the Austronesian family run 900-1200 languages because it is hard to draw the line between dialect and language, a callback to the Chuukic “language limit” from Tuesday.
Possible student answers to the Discuss (my synthesis, not Schütz’s claims; Schütz says only that language “still provides the most important data”). It’s fine to push back on “most important”: the strongest answer is that the lines of evidence complement each other.

Pottery and carbon dates tell us what and when, not who or how. Lapita sherds and radiocarbon dates date a site but say nothing about what people spoke or who they were related to. Language links people to people.
Pottery doesn’t last. Many Polynesian islands stopped making pottery, so the trail goes cold just where we most need it.
Language is carried by people, not objects. Words can’t be traded like pots, and a language is learned from other speakers, so it records real contact and descent. (Vocabulary can be borrowed, which is why linguists weight core vocabulary and sound correspondences.)
Sound correspondences are systematic. Regular patterns like k/t and h/f/wh are very hard to get by chance or borrowing, so they give a testable family tree.
Language can be compared across the whole family. We can line up 30+ languages across thousands of miles, which no single archaeological site allows.
DNA shows ancestry, not speech. Genes can show who mixed with whom, but not which language they spoke. Peoples sometimes shift languages and keep their genes, or the reverse.
No single source is enough. Each can mislead on its own. Early glottochronology dates and the Cook/Waimea impression of “one language” later in the deck are cautionary tales. The strongest conclusions come when language, archaeology, and DNA agree, and the live debates come when they don’t (see “Still Debated”).

title: The Languages of Polynesia
text:
Spices, Sailors, and Word Lists

Europeans first met Polynesian languages through the spice trade: the quest for cloves, mace, nutmeg, and pepper, controlled by Venetian merchants, drove ships to look for new routes
In 1615-16, Dutch partners Willem Schouten and Isaac Le Maire sailed to find a new route to the East Indies. Their crew had scurvy, and in May 1616 they reached islands near Vava’u in the Tonga group
Le Maire’s son Iacob collected 32 words from Tafahi and 118 words from East Futuna — the first written sample of a Polynesian language in Europe
The lists were useless for talking to other islanders: later explorers (Abel Tasman) tried them on Māori and Tongan with little success


Schütz, pp. 97-98. Point out the “voyages of discovery” framing: the discoveries were a byproduct of a commercial motive.

title: The Languages of Polynesia
text:
Reland Spots the Pattern (1706)

Dutch scholar Hadrian Reland compared the Tafahi/East Futuna words with Malay and saw similarities “too striking to be coincidental”
His idea: languages as far apart as Tonga and the Malay Peninsula and Madagascar belong to one family, later called Malayo-Polynesian, now a subgroup of Austronesian
Captain James Cook’s voyages (later 1700s) confirmed it. His naturalists published a comparative table of numerals for 39 languages showing the “affinity and extent of language”


Schütz, pp. 98-99. Reland proposed this more than 60 years before Cook; Cook’s data confirmed it.

title: The Languages of Polynesia
text:
What’s in the Name “Polynesia”?

Charles de Brosses coined the term in his 1756 Histoire, dividing the Pacific into three parts and naming the third “Polynesia,” from Greek polus ‘many’ + nēsos ‘island’
Even the name had a commercial motive: de Brosses wanted to suggest that the Pacific might hide “a large number of islands rich in spiceries”


Discuss: We use “Polynesia,” “Micronesia,” and “Melanesia” as if they were natural categories. What does it mean that they come from European explorers and mapmakers? (Callback to Tuesday: culture areas are defined by peoples and languages, not borders on a map.)


Schütz, p. 100. Ties back to the “What Is a Culture Area?” slide in the Micronesia deck. Tcherkézoff (2003) is the source Schütz cites for the de Brosses quotation.

title: The Languages of Polynesia
text:
Which Way Did They Sail?



For years the settlement of the Pacific was assumed to run west to east. Thor Heyerdahl argued the opposite: that Polynesia was settled from South America, and sailed the Kon-Tiki (1947) to show it could be done
He proved an east-to-west trip was possible, but evidence from several fields still pointed overwhelmingly to west-to-east migration
That doesn’t mean there was no contact with South America. Blust: the sweet potato (Ipomoea batatas) in the Pacific before Columbus shows contact, but it is evidence of voyagers from the Pacific reaching South America, not the reverse
Even further back: isotope analysis of stone tools shows people crossing 100 miles of open water from the South China coast to the Penghu Islands in the Taiwan Strait, “the first stage of Austronesian seafaring” (Jiao, quoted in Krauss 2006)





The Kon-Tiki raft, Kon-Tiki Museum, Oslo




Schütz, pp. 101-102. Good place to remind students that the same evidence base (archaeology, DNA, language) keeps revising the story.

How many? One scholar counts 53 speech communities grouped into 26 languages (Biggs 1971), but other counts differ, since the line between dialect and language is hazy
What are they called? Clark (1979) lists 34 names





The Polynesian triangle




Schütz, pp. 101-102. The same dialect/language problem we hit with the Chuukic continuum on Tuesday.

title: The Languages of Polynesia
text:
Same Language, or Different?



In 1769 Captain Cook left Tahiti for Aotearoa with Tupaia, a Tahitian priest, adviser, and navigator. When they met the Māori, Tupaia called out “in the language of Otaheite” and the Māori seemed to understand
In 1778, Hawaiians at Waimea, Kaua’i, understood the Tahitian some of Cook’s crew spoke. Samwell wrote the language was “the same as that of Otaheite”
That gave rise to the idea that Polynesians spoke one language with dialects. Even missionary linguists like John Davies, who wrote a Tahitian dictionary, used the singular
But the “perfect understanding” was only the Europeans’ impression. Schütz: it was probably “a communication of simple ideas, enhanced by gestures”





Tupaia’s map, c. 1769




Discuss: Why might first-time visitors have overestimated how well the languages were understood across islands?


Schütz, p. 103. Cook’s crew had reasons to hear similarity (they wanted trade and fresh supplies), and the dialect/language question is still unsettled. Note Schütz’s later point: the Waimea ease of understanding may actually be evidence for continued contact, or later settlement (see the When slide).

The Family Tree





flowchart LR
  PP["Proto-Polynesian"] --> TG["Proto-Tongic"]
  PP --> NP["Proto-Nuclear Polynesian"]
  TG --> T["Tongan, Niuean"]
  NP --> SO["Proto-Samoic-Outlier"]
  NP --> EP["Proto-East Polynesian"]
  SO --> S["Samoan, Tokelauan, Tūvalu, Pukapuka... and the Outliers: Nukuoro, Kapingamarangi, Tikopia, Sikaiana, Rennellese..."]

  CE --> C["Hawaiian, Marquesan, Tahitian, Māori, Rarotongan, Tuamotuan, Mangareva..."]







Schütz Figure 3 (Clark 1979, based on Pawley 1966). Key points: (1) Tongan and Niuean branch off first; (2) Samoan sits with a group that includes most Outliers, so Nukuoro and Kapingamarangi are closer to Samoan than to Hawaiian; (3) Hawaiian is in East Polynesian, with Rapanui as the separate branch. Before Pawley (1966), scholars split Polynesian geographically into East vs. West, with Tongan and Samoan together as Western. Pawley’s grammatical innovations broke that up: a good example of language family evidence overriding geography, same lesson as Tuesday.

title: The Languages of Polynesia
text:
Reworking the Tree

Linguist Mary Walworth (2014) argues the Tahitic and Marquesic subgroups were “based on weak evidence” and removes them, using archaeology and linguistics together
Her revised tree puts most Eastern Polynesian languages (Hawaiian, Tahitian, Marquesan, Māori…) in one Central Eastern group with no finer internal grouping. Rapanui is the only branch that really developed in isolation
Why: most Eastern Polynesian languages seem to have developed in contact with each other, which matches archaeological evidence for rapid settlement and ongoing exchange


Discuss: If languages keep influencing each other after they split, how well does a tree describe them?


Schütz, pp. 106-107. Walworth’s evidence for a “wave” (contact) model rather than a clean branching tree. Zotero has Walworth 2014 if you want the original. Optional callback if you’ve covered the tree vs. wave models of language change earlier in the course (e.g., François, “Trees, Waves and Linkages”).

title: The Languages of Polynesia
section: Still Debated: Where Did Eastern Polynesian Come From?
text:
Still Debated: Where Did Eastern Polynesian Come From?
Two linguists, same question, different answers:


Walworth (2014): the languages grew together

New radiocarbon dates suggest eastern Polynesia was settled late and fast
Too little time for a neat branching tree; people kept trading and talking across islands
Shared features spread by contact, not just inheritance


Wilson (2021): look to the northwest

Eastern Polynesian’s closest relatives are tiny Outlier atolls (Takuu, Nukumanu, Luangiua, Nukeria) northeast of New Guinea, in the Bougainville and Solomon Islands area
Homeland: somewhere around the Phoenix, Line, and Marquesas Islands
Hawaiian may descend from its own northern branch, not from a Marquesan or Tahitian one



Discuss: Both use word comparisons. Why can smart people looking at the same words still disagree? What other evidence (archaeology, DNA, navigation) would you want?


Ties back to Back to Waimea and the settlement-date table: new dates + new linguistic models are still reshaping the story. Hawaiian’s closest relatives are an open question; there is no consensus. Keep it conceptual, no reconstruction details. The point for 100-level: linguistics is an active field, and “how closely related” depends on whether you model splitting (tree) or contact (wave). Walworth, M. 2014. “Eastern Polynesian: The Linguistic Evidence Revisited.” Oceanic Linguistics 53(2): 256-272 (uses Wilmshurst et al. 2011 radiocarbon dates). Wilson, W. H. 2021. “East Polynesian Subgrouping and Homeland Implications Within the Northern Outlier-East Polynesian Hypothesis.” Oceanic Linguistics 60(1): 36-71. Wilson explicitly contests the Walworth contact-network model (his section 8). Wilson’s paper is 37 pages of reconstructed forms; do not assign it. Say “Walworth vs. Wilson” only if students ask who is behind each view.

Glottochronology assumes basic vocabulary changes at a roughly fixed rate. Too variable to trust alone (e.g., the Tahitian practice of pi’i, word replacement, changed vocabulary faster than expected)
Linguistic dates only become useful when checked against carbon-14 dating and oral genealogies


Schütz, pp. 108-110. Sources for each row as cited by Schütz. Carbon-14 dates cited: A.D. 818-1190; genealogy date A.D. 1050. Hunt (via Kubota 2011): Polynesians reached Samoa and Tonga about 800 B.C., then moved east again about A.D. 1100, settling Tahiti and the rest of eastern Polynesia between A.D. 1200 and 1300, helped by improved vessels and favorable El Niño winds.

title: The Languages of Polynesia
text:
Back to Waimea
Remember Cook’s crew understanding the Hawaiians at Waimea? A later settlement date changes how we read that story:



If Hawai’i was settled late, Tahitian and Hawaiian haven’t had long to drift apart
Or there was continued contact between Hawai’i and its relatives to the south. Schütz: current opinion dismisses the idea that Hawai’i was reached once and then stayed isolated
Origins: archaeology, linguistics, anthropology, and ethnobotany point to the Marquesas as the immediate homeland of the first settlers (Kirch), with Tahiti connections coming later, and possibly more than one voyage
DNA points the same way: a common lineage spread across the Pacific, which geneticist Rebecca Cann says could only happen with constant contact. In her words: “The Polynesians used the ocean as a superhighway”





Hōkūle’a, Honolulu




Discuss: Hōkūle’a and Hawai’iloa have shown that long voyages work. How does that change what you thought “isolated islands” meant?


Schütz, pp. 109-110. Closing thought: modern technology (DNA, redated archaeological sites) is bringing earlier events into sharper focus, even as time moves them further away. Schütz also notes DNA evidence for occasional voyages east to South America, not just west to east.

title: The Languages of Polynesia
text:
Three Questions Linguists Ask
Comparing Polynesian languages pair by pair, scholars ask:

How much do speakers of the two languages understand each other?
How many basic words do they share?
When did the languages split, when did speakers lose contact?

The third question needs both linguistic and non-linguistic evidence.

Exit ticket (3 min): Pick one of today’s three ways of measuring closeness (understanding, shared words, or sound correspondences). What does it tell us, and what does it miss?


Schütz, pp. 110-111. Collect on the way out, or use as the next Journal prompt.

title: Borrowing (cont.) and Midterm Review
section: Language Nests and the Purist Turn
text:
Language Nests and the Purist Turn
Language planning = making and enforcing decisions on language use: education, writing systems, translators, and which words to use for new concepts.

In the 1800s, nearly all Pacific language planning was done by religious organizations
Hawaiian and Māori seemed headed for extinction ~50 years ago. Activists set up immersion preschools, language nests: kōhanga reo (Aotearoa, 1982) and pūnana leo (Hawaiʻi, 1983), which grew into schools and universities
Adults wanted to use the language at home and work, so they needed thousands of new words. The Polynesian Languages Forum (1991) coordinated this
Most activists wanted to distance the language from colonial languages: avoid loans as much as possible, build words by compounding and expansion

Computer: kamepiula (loan) or lolouila (lolo ‘brain’ + uila ‘electricity’)? Māori: rorohiko (roro ‘brain’ + hiko ‘spark’).

Debate (3 min): Is a “purist” policy good for a small language, when borrowing is a natural process?


Geraghty, pp. 173-174 (section 11); also see Schütz (1994:361-377) for Hawaiian and Holmes (2001), Harlow (2004) for Aotearoa. Māmaka Kaiao lists lolouila (‘computer’, lolo + uila) alongside kamepiula, and Harlow’s chapter in Tent & Geraghty (2004) lists Māori rorohiko. DISCUSSION POINTS (no single answer): for purism: identity, distance from colonialism, transparency (lolouila explains itself), and learnable vocabulary for children in immersion schools. Against purism: borrowing is natural, speeds up coining, and keeps the language connected to the everyday life of speakers who also use English. The next slide shows the Hawaiian Lexicon Committee’s own guidelines, a practical middle path.

title: Borrowing (cont.) and Midterm Review
section: How Does a Committee Make a Word?
text:
How Does a Committee Make a Word?
The Hawaiian Lexicon Committee (founded 1987; kūpuna and native speakers from the start) meets 4-6 times a year. Every word must be approved at two meetings. Their dictionary, Māmaka Kaiao, records ten strategies:







Strategy
Example




Describe the concept in Hawaiian words
uila mahu pele ‘geothermal electricity’ (‘electricity-steam-volcano’)


Combine words
poelele ‘satellite’ (poe ‘buoy’ + lele ‘fly’); hamulau ‘herbivore’ (hamu ‘to chew’ + lau ‘leaf’)


Shorten and combine
ikehu ‘energy’ (ika ‘strength’ + ehu ‘lively’)


Add affixes
kalaianiau ‘climatology’ (kalai- ‘study of’ + aniau ‘climate’)


Extend an old word
haumia ‘pollution’ (old word ‘defiled, unclean’); hoʻoili ‘download’ (hoʻo- ‘cause’ + ili ‘transfer’; also ‘transplant’)


Borrow from another Polynesian language
pounamu ‘jade’ (Māori); makahiʻo ‘explore’ (maka ‘eye’ + Tahitian hiʻo ‘look’)


Hawaiianize a foreign word
naelona ‘nylon’; kaimine ‘saimin’ (Japanese); kokeiʻa ‘prairie dog’ (Ute); ʻōmā ‘lobster’ (French homard)




Discuss: The committee builds first but still borrows. Is that purism? What would you call it?


From the English introduction to Māmaka Kaiao (Hawaiian Lexicon Committee; 2003 edition, with the vocabulary created 1987-2000). The introduction lists ten guidelines; the table gives seven. Others: make minor changes to an existing word (adding a kahakō), record words native speakers already use, and use reduplication (ulialia ‘coincidence’). ANSWER / TALKING POINT: it is a pragmatic mix, not strict purism. The committee prefers Hawaiian resources, then other Polynesian languages, and only then Hawaiianizes non-Polynesian words. This is the “build or borrow” choice made by a community committee instead of missionaries. The component glosses on the table: poelele (‘flying buoy’), hamulau (hamu + lau), kalaianiau (kalai- + aniau), haumia and hoʻoili (existing words with extended meanings) are from the dictionary entries in Māmaka Kaiao; ika ‘strength’, ehu ‘lively’, hamu ‘to chew’, and ili ‘transfer’ are from general Hawaiian knowledge, so check them against Pukui and Elbert before class. WOLD’s Hawaiian list includes many committee words as loans (source “Kōmike Huaʻōlelo 2003”), e.g., puolo ‘music’ from Māori puoro.

title: Borrowing (cont.) and Midterm Review
text:
Putting It Together: Borrowing







Question
Answer




What is borrowing?
Sounds, words, endings, structures, meanings copied from another language; not code-switching


Why borrow?
Needed (new things) or intimate (close contact); also prestige


What are the alternatives?
Compounding, semantic expansion, calques


What happens to loans?
Sound adaptation, semantic shift, reanalysis


What gets borrowed?
Nouns > verbs/adjectives > function words; introduced things (WOLD data); body and kin words mostly not


Who decides?
Missionaries, communities, language planners: borrow or build?




Exit ticket (2 min): Pick one loanword (from Tuesday, or one you use). What does it tell us about the relationship between the two languages, and how was it adapted?


Terms that could appear on Quiz #4: borrowing, loanword, calque, code-switching, semantic expansion, compounding, semantic shift, reanalysis, etymological borrowing, intimate vs. cultural borrowing. SAMPLE EXIT-TICKET ANSWERS: (a) pipi (Hawaiian) from English beef: cattle came through contact with English speakers; /b f/ became /p p/ and a final vowel was added; the meaning extended from meat to the animal. (b) Kula ‘school’: a missionary-era loan; a vowel was added after the final consonant. (c) Pork in English: French-derived, showing French-speaking elites ate the meat. Accept any loan with a reasonable claim about the contact and a sound or meaning change.

Quick-Fire Recap (5 min)
With a partner. 20 seconds each. No notes.

What is the strongest evidence that two languages are related, not borrowed?
A change shared by some languages but not others is a shared ______.
Match: Hawaiian, Tok Pisin, English in Fiji, Fiji Hindi to Lynch’s categories.
Which factor explains diversity if groups stay apart for a long time?
A pidgin has no ______ speakers.
Which language shaped Pidgin’s grammar more: Japanese or Portuguese?
What do yumi and mifala show (first person plural pronouns in Melanesian English Creoles; we)?


ANSWERS: (1) regular sound correspondences across many basic words (not a few similar-sounding words); (2) innovation; (3) Hawaiian is indigenous; Tok Pisin is pidgin/creole; English in Fiji is metropolitan; Fiji Hindi is immigrant (Fiji Hindi arose from indentured laborers; some textbooks also treat it as a creole-like koiné, so accept a justified answer); (4) separation (and time); (5) native; (6) pidgins can develop with no European input; (7) Portuguese, despite the much larger Japanese group (look up the reasons in your Oct 15 slides and Sakoda & Siegel; I did not include them here); (8) the inclusive/exclusive “we” distinction, probably from the Oceanic substrate languages of Vanuatu, which shows that Bislama’s grammar is not English with endings dropped. Note: question 3’s Fiji Hindi answer is the one most likely to produce debate. Use five minutes total, then take a few volunteers.

ANSWERS: (a) Hawaiian h : Samoan f (ahi : afi); Hawaiian k : Samoan t (koko : toto); also Hawaiian w : Samoan v (waʻa : vaʻa), and Hawaiian ʻ (glottal stop) matches Samoan ʻ in some words. (c) Cognates: the same correspondences hold across several basic words (fire, blood, canoe, five), which is regular, so it is inheritance from a common ancestor, not copying. (d) Suspect borrowing if a word breaks the regular pattern (for example, Hawaiian k matching Samoan k), if it names a recent or introduced thing, or if it sits outside basic vocabulary; borrowing can also produce regular matches (see the etymological borrowing example from Tuesday’s hidden slides), so combine with other evidence. Practice 2: Reading Bislama (7 min)

Mifala i talem se Jeni i stap. ‘We said that Jenny was here.’


Yumi go. (‘Let’s go: you and me’) vs. Mifala i go. (‘We go: not you’)

In pairs:

Which words come from English? Which grammar is not English?
What is the i before the verb? What is se?
Which “we” is used in the first sentence? Why does that matter?
Someone says “Bislama is just broken English.” Answer in two sentences.


Example from Meyerhoff, pp. 146-147 (examples (4)-(7)); the second line is built from the yumi / mifala distinction on the substrate slide (pidgins.qmd), not quoted from the chapter, so check it against your slides. ANSWERS: (a) English-derived: talem (tell + -em), se (say); not English: the i agreement marker before the verb, the transitive suffix -em, and se used to introduce a clause. (b) i is a predicate (agreement) marker before the verb (Meyerhoff glosses it AGR) that matches Oceanic languages of Vanuatu, not English; se (‘say’) introduces a clause, as in many Oceanic languages. (c) Mifala is the exclusive “we” (the listener is not included), a distinction English lacks, which shows the substrate shaped Bislama’s grammar. (d) Bislama has its own grammar, built from Vanuatu languages as well as English vocabulary, so it is not English with errors; “broken” is an attitude, not a linguistic description (Meyerhoff: “simple” is not “broken”).

Practice 3: From Pidgin to Creole in Hawaiʻi (7 min)







Date
Event




1835
First sugar plantation opens. Hawaiians still rule; Hawaiian is the language of government and of schooling for non-European children


1852-76
About 2,000 laborers from China arrive (mostly Cantonese speakers)


1878-87
More than 10,000 laborers from Portugal arrive


1884-1924
Over 200,000 laborers from Japan arrive


About 1900
The first locally born Chinese and Portuguese children appear; many are spoken to in Pidgin English as newborns


1920-30

In pairs:

Which language was the basis of the first plantation pidgin? What in the timeline explains that?
Give one piece of evidence that a creole existed by about 1920. What makes it a creole, not a pidgin?
A friend says “Pidgin never changed: it’s just plantation English.” Use the timeline to answer in two sentences.


Practice item built from the Oct 15 deck (Sakoda & Siegel, pp. 153-157); no Hawaiian or Pidgin reading is needed, so it tests concepts instead of language skills. ANSWERS: (a) Hawaiian: Hawaiians still ruled in 1835, and Hawaiian was the language of government and of schooling for non-European children, so it became the language used to run the plantations (Pidgin Hawaiian came first, then English-based pidgin). (b) Locally born children acquiring it from birth (about 1900 onward, and by 1920-30 locally born children equal or outnumber the foreign born): a creole has native speakers and a full range of functions, while a pidgin is learned as a second language and used in limited situations. (c) It changed in stages: Hawaiian-based pidgin, then English-based pidgin, then a creole spoken as a first language by children who added new grammar (for example never, stay, for). It is its own language with its own grammar, not “English with errors.” Optional extension: why did Portuguese influence the grammar more than the larger Japanese group? (Use the Oct 15 deck.)

Planning an Essay Together (8 min)
Prompt: How can linguists use language evidence to work out how Pacific peoples spread across the islands? Use at least two kinds of evidence and two examples.








Piece
What goes here
Source to use




Thesis
What language can (and cannot) tell us



Evidence 1
Regular sound correspondences: relatedness, not borrowing



Evidence 2
Shared innovations: subgroups and the family tree



Example
Austronesian from Taiwan; the Polynesian tree; Pawley (1966); Outliers



Limits
Geography, culture areas, and “Papuan” are not language families





Rule of thumb: each paragraph = one claim, one example, one “so what.”


Chosen so it is not one of the three exam essay options (Melanesian vs. Polynesian diversity; “Pidgin is just broken English”; Bislama vs. Hawaiian Pidgin). It pulls from Weeks 1-3, 5, and 7. Fill in the table on the board with the class. Sample answers: Thesis: regular patterns in vocabulary and shared changes let linguists reconstruct family trees and the order of settlement, but language evidence must be combined with archaeology and cannot be read off a map. Evidence 1: regular sound correspondences (Hawaiian k : Samoan t, h : f) across many basic words show common descent; a few look-alike words could be borrowing. Evidence 2: a shared innovation, not a shared retention, shows a subgroup; this gives the tree (Tongic, Nuclear Polynesian, Samoic-Outlier, East Polynesian). Example: Austronesian stretches from Madagascar to Rapa Nui and is traced to Taiwan; Pawley (1966) showed Polynesian languages do not split into simple western vs. eastern groups; Polynesian Outliers sit far from where their relatives are. Limits: culture areas (Micronesia, Polynesia, Melanesia) do not line up with language families; “Papuan” is a negative label, not a family; mutual intelligibility is not the same as shared cognates. Check each point against your Weeks 1-7 lectures.
HOW TO RUN IT (8 min). Do not teach the five-paragraph essay: the exam essay is two to three paragraphs, so use one paragraph pattern (claim, example, so what). (1) Read the prompt and underline the verbs (1 min): “use evidence” and “at least two kinds” are the grading criteria; a specific thesis plus specific evidence beats length. (2) Thesis (1.5 min): one sentence that answers the prompt, not one that repeats it. Weak: “Language tells us a lot about how people moved.” Stronger: “Regular sound correspondences and shared innovations let linguists reconstruct how Polynesia was settled, but they work best alongside archaeology.” Take one or two volunteer attempts. (3) Fill the table with the class (3.5 min): cold-call a pair per row, or give each pair two rows; for each row ask “where in your notes is this?” (open notes help you find an answer). (4) Map it to two or three paragraphs (1 min): thesis + Evidence 1 + example = one paragraph; Evidence 2 + example = a second; limits + “so what” = a third, or folded into the second if time is short. (5) Time check (1 min): the essay is worth 20 points and gets about 20 minutes: about 3 to plan, 15 to write, 2 to reread. The most common mistake is writing without planning, which leads to a repeated point or a missing example.
ALSO SAY: name the evidence (“Hawaiian k : Samoan t” beats “the languages are similar”). Point at the exam’s three real options and tell them to spend 2 minutes choosing, not 10. Homework: outline one of the three actual options (or this one) without notes, then check against the review sheet; don’t outline an actual option in class, since that would leak exam content. If they finish early: 90 seconds to underline in their notes which row was hardest to fill.

title: The Languages of Micronesia
text:
Just How Big Is Micronesia?
Bender’s own way of putting it:

Fly from Los Angeles to Hawai’i, then keep going the same distance again in the same direction — you’d land in Majuro, Marshall Islands, just past the International Date Line
Crossing Micronesia east to west, from Majuro to Palau, is roughly the distance from New York to California — about 3,000 miles
And most of what’s in between is, as Bender puts it, barely specks on a map — this region’s name literally means “small islands”



Quick opening hook before the map. Helps students viscerally grasp that “Micronesia” isn’t one tight cluster of islands, it’s an area the size of the continental US, just almost entirely ocean.

title: The Languages of Micronesia
text:
What Is a “Culture Area”?


Micronesia, Melanesia, and Polynesia — the three areas we’ve been using all semester — aren’t geographic or political categories.

They’re defined by indigenous peoples and their ways of living, including their languages — not by neat boundaries on a map
We’ll see this complicate things today: Chamorro and Palauan aren’t even Oceanic languages, and two Polynesian languages (Kapingamarangi, Nukuoro) are spoken deep inside Micronesia
Keep an eye out for how often “which culture area is this?” and “which language family is this?” give different answers

title: The Languages of Micronesia
text:
Living on a Life Raft
Almost 2 in 5 Micronesians live on coral atolls — a sliver of land, often under a mile wide, a few feet above sea level at most. That environment leaves a mark on the language.


Atoll languages are unusually rich in vocabulary for:

Navigation, stars, and wayfinding
Fishing methods, canoe parts and sailing
Coconut, breadfruit, and pandanus cultivation


High-island languages are richer instead in:

Names for flora and fauna
Topographical features (ridges, valleys, streams)


When atoll families resettle on high islands — Mortlock Islanders on Pohnpei, Satawal Islanders on Saipan — their children often stop acquiring that specialized atoll vocabulary within a generation or two.

Discuss: If you grew up on a high island and moved to an atoll (or vice versa), what vocabulary do you think would be hardest to pick up?


This is the richest unused material in the chapter and connects directly back to Kale’s ecology question and the Abui classification material from Tuesday — language tracks environment, and that knowledge is genuinely fragile across a single generation of relocation.

Settled from the Philippines around 1500 BC — one of the longest open-ocean voyages (1,300 mi.) in the entire Austronesian expansion, until Polynesians later crossed even farther
Belongs to the first wave of Austronesian migration out of Taiwan, the same wave that settled the Philippines and Indonesia — a completely separate branch from the Oceanic languages of Melanesia/Polynesia we’ve covered so far

Good opening move: most students will assume “Pacific Islander language” = Oceanic by default. Chamorro breaks that pattern immediately and is worth flagging explicitly.

Just as Spanish left its mark on Chamorro, Japanese left its mark on Palauan.



Japan administered Palau from 1914 to 1944 and introduced Japanese-language schooling right away
Hundreds of Japanese loanwords entered everyday Palauan (one study counts 850+), and many are still in use today, though fewer than a generation ago
Japanese rule also brought surnames into common use — civil records like birth certificates, marriage licenses, and inheritance required them

FSM 🇫🇲
The Federated States of Micronesia is four states, each with its own language — and those four languages fall into two very different linguistic categories.


Yapese stands alone — an early, separate branch of Oceanic (~1400 BC), not part of the “Nuclear Micronesian” group the other three belong to.

Chuukese, Pohnpeian, and Kosraean are all Nuclear Micronesian — descended from one shared ancestor, Proto-Micronesian, that spread out from the eastern end of Micronesia.



Set up the two sub-threads before diving into states individually: (1) Yap is the outlier, (2) the other three share deep common ancestry. This primes the Chuukic-continuum material coming up under Chuuk.

title: The Languages of Micronesia

Yap


Yapese stands alone among the FSM’s languages — possibly linked to the Admiralty Islands, not part of “Nuclear Micronesian” at all.

The high island of Yap has historically provided famine relief to its surrounding atolls (Ulithi, Woleai, etc.) during typhoons — a tribute relationship sometimes called the Yap Empire
Those outer-atoll languages (Ulithian, Woleaian, Satawalese, and others) are actually part of the Chuukic continuum — more on that next

title: The Languages of Micronesia
text:
Pohnpei



Pohnpeian is part of the Pohnpeic branch of Nuclear Micronesian, with its own satellite atoll languages (Mokilese, Pingilapese, Ngatikese)
Two unrelated Polynesian Outlier languages — Kapingamarangi and Nukuoro — are also spoken in Pohnpei State, despite being geographically deep in Micronesia. Their speakers arrived via Tuvalu around 1000 AD
Nan Madol — the massive stone ruins on Pohnpei — may be linked to the rise of an early, breadfruit-fueled Micronesian society




Nan Madol ruins, Pohnpei



Discuss: Kapingamarangi and Nukuoro are Polynesian languages spoken in Micronesia. What does that tell us about the difference between a geographic region and a linguistic one?

title: The Languages of Micronesia
text:
Kosrae



Kosraean may be the closest thing to a “homeland” for all of Nuclear Micronesian — genetic-tree evidence (Ross 1996) points to Kosrae as the likely point of origin
It’s the only high island among the four easternmost points of Micronesia (with Nauru, northern Kiribati, and the southern Marshalls) — more land, fresh water, and room for sustained settlement than an atoll offers
Lelu, Kosrae’s own set of stone ruins, parallels Nan Madol on Pohnpei

title: The Languages of Micronesia
text: Marshall Islands 🇲🇭

title: The Languages of Micronesia
text:
Marshall Islands 🇲🇭
Bender uses Marshallese as the chapter’s showcase for Nuclear Micronesian grammar — a few standout features:



Two words for “we”, depending on whether the listener is included or not (inclusive vs. exclusive)
An elaborate demonstrative system layered on person (“close to me” vs. “close to you” vs. “close to someone else”) and human/nonhuman distinctions
Directional suffixes that fuse onto verbs for compass directions, sea vs. land, even “toward the lagoon” vs. “toward the ocean side”




Marshallese stick chart (directional/wave navigation)


A Marshallese language commissioner, writing to Bender about the capital Majuro, describes watching Marshallese (Kajin Ṃajeḷ, “KM”) lose ground to English (Kajin Pālle, “KP”) in real time: code-mixed parliamentary debates, kids raised in English when one parent isn’t Marshallese, phone numbers given in English even by people who know the Marshallese words, DVDs flooding households with English.

Discuss: The commissioner calls this “the beginning of the demise of KM.” Compare this to what we discussed last class about Bislama and Vanuatu’s indigenous languages — same mechanism, different island group?


This quote is genuinely moving in context — consider reading it aloud rather than summarizing. Strong bridge back to Tuesday’s Vanuatu/Bislama material and the Abui semantic-convergence slide; same underlying process (urbanization, a dominant contact/colonial language, generational break in transmission) recurring across completely different parts of the Pacific.

title: The Languages of Micronesia
text: Nauru (Naoero) 🇳🇷

title: The Languages of Micronesia
text:
Nauru (Naoero) 🇳🇷

The world’s smallest independent nation — just 8 sq. mi.
Nauruan is Nuclear Micronesian, but highly distinct from its nearest relatives — had it been included in the 2003 Proto-Micronesian reconstruction study, it likely would have formed its own top-level branch, just like Kosraean, Marshallese, and Kiribati each do
Together, Nauru, Kosrae, the southern Marshalls, and northern Kiribati form a roughly 500-mile “quadrilateral” that’s the best candidate for where Nuclear Micronesian first took root

title: The Languages of Micronesia

title: The Languages of Micronesia
text:
Kiribati 🇰🇮

Likely the first landfall of the Nuclear Micronesian migration out of the southeast Solomons — a 1,100-mile voyage, around 3,000 years ago
Entirely atolls — no point in the country rises more than 33 ft. above sea level
A live, current existential threat: when Bender wrote this chapter, Kiribati had purchased land in Fiji and President Anote Tong was framing eventual relocation as “migration with dignity.”
Kiribati’s current president, Taneti Maamau (reelected 2024), has taken the opposite approach: rather than planning to relocate, his government is pursuing large-scale land reclamation and dredging — physically raising and expanding the islands, backed by Chinese aid — to stay in place
Either way — relocating or raising the land — much of the atoll-specific vocabulary (navigation, fishing, canoe parts, star names) is tied to a way of life that’s already under pressure


Discuss: Two very different responses to the same threat — leave, or raise the land. What might each one mean for the long-term survival of the language?


Updated from Bender’s original framing: Tong’s “migration with dignity” was the policy in place when the chapter was written, but Maamau has since reversed course. Good moment to note that even a 2012-ish chapter can go out of date on fast-moving political material — model that kind of source-checking for students.

title: The Languages of Micronesia
section: Activity: Relocate or Raise the Land? (12 min)
text:
Activity: Relocate or Raise the Land? (12 min)
Form groups of 4. Each group is assigned a side (split the room in half):


Team Relocate
Kiribati should plan for “migration with dignity” — resettle its people abroad over time.

Team Raise the Land
Kiribati should stay: dredge, reclaim, and raise the islands.

Your job (6 min): make the best case for your side using language and culture survival as your main criterion. Draw on today’s slides:

Atoll vocabulary tied to a way of life (Living on a Life Raft)
Marshallese in Majuro vs. Springdale, Arkansas
Carolinian on Saipan; Mortlock Islanders on Pohnpei

Then (6 min): pair with a group from the other side. Each side gets 90 seconds, then you try to find one point of agreement.

Timing: ~1 min set-up, 6 min prep, 6 min cross-group pairing, ~3 min whole-class debrief (total about 12-15 min). Debrief questions: What did each side have to assume about language survival? Does a language need a place? Who gets to decide, and who was left out of the policy debate? Remind students this is a live political question for real communities, so aim for good-faith argument, not mockery. Tie directly into the exit ticket right after. A source worth having handy: coverage of Maamau’s land-reclamation plans and Tong’s “migration with dignity” (the Kiribati slide above already summarizes both).

title: The Languages of Micronesia
text:
Modern-Day Pressures
Across all of Micronesia, the same underlying forces are reshaping language use, regardless of which specific islands or languages are involved:

Rapid urbanization — Majuro, Koror, Weno, Kolonia — pulls people off outer islands and atolls into crowded town centers
A cash economy replaces subsistence fishing/farming, and with it, the specialized vocabulary tied to those practices
English spreads through schooling, media, and intermarriage, often becoming the de facto home language for the next generation
The US military presence at Kwajalein (Marshall Islands) is its own distinct pressure — a missile testing range that has reshaped Marshallese land use and labor for decades


Synthesis slide pulling together Bender’s §8 “Modern-Day Micronesia” material — meant to generalize the Marshallese KM/KP story so students see it as a regional pattern, not a one-off.

title: The Languages of Micronesia
text:
The Compact of Free Association (COFA)
The FSM, the Marshall Islands, and Palau are independent nations, but each has a Compact of Free Association with the US — not colonies, but closely bound by treaty.

Citizens of all three can live, work, and study in the US without a visa — this is why Micronesian communities exist across the US mainland and Hawai’i
COFA funding was renewed in 2024: $7.1 billion over 20 years ($3.3B to FSM, $2.3B to RMI, $889M to Palau). Separately, Medicaid eligibility for COFA citizens living in the US was restored by Congress in December 2020, after being cut off by the 1996 welfare reform law
This free-movement relationship is a major driver of the diaspora communities we’re about to look at

title: The Languages of Micronesia
text:
The Marshallese Diaspora: Springdale, Arkansas

Springdale is now home to an estimated 12,000-15,000 Marshallese residents — the largest Marshallese community outside the Marshall Islands themselves
Drawn originally by poultry-industry jobs, enabled by COFA’s visa-free travel
The community has built real institutional infrastructure: more than 30 Marshallese churches, a Marshallese-language radio station, and an RMI consulate — the only one in the continental US
An open question for a diaspora this size: does that infrastructure make it easier to maintain Kajin Ṃajeḷ across generations than it’s been in Majuro itself, where English pressure is also intense?


Discuss: Compare Springdale to the Chamorro/Carolinian bilingualism on Saipan, or to the KM/KP situation in Majuro. Does moving away from the homeland always mean faster language loss — or could it sometimes mean the opposite?


Deliberately leaves this open — there’s a real research question here about whether concentrated diaspora communities with their own institutions can sometimes outperform the homeland at heritage-language maintenance. Good forward pointer to Week 11 (language endangerment/maintenance).

title: The Languages of Micronesia
section: Closer to Home: Micronesians in Hawai’i
text:
Closer to Home: Micronesians in Hawai’i
Hawai’i is home to a large COFA migrant community — and the discrimination against it is well documented.

A 2019 U.S. Commission on Civil Rights report found Micronesian migrants face substantial barriers to housing, employment, healthcare, and education in Hawai’i — including landlords who refuse to rent to them and employers who won’t hire them
Health coverage: the 1996 federal welfare reform law cut COFA migrants off from Medicaid. Around 2010 Hawai’i moved them to a more limited state-funded plan, and in 2014 the Ninth Circuit (Korab v. Fink) held the state wasn’t required to make up the lost federal funding. Congress only restored Medicaid eligibility in December 2020
COVID-19: Pacific Islanders (a category that includes Micronesians) were about 5% of Hawai’i’s population but about 22% of cases from March 2020 to February 2021 — an infection rate roughly 4.8 times the state average (7,070 vs. 1,477 per 100,000)
UH Mānoa’s own Thompson School of Social Work has studied discrimination directly, documenting Micronesians being stereotyped in local public discourse as “dirty,” “uneducated,” or a drain on the healthcare and welfare systems — stereotypes not supported by the data on actual service use


Discuss: We’ve spent today’s class treating Micronesian languages and peoples as subjects of academic study. What’s it like to realize this community’s everyday experience, here in the state where many of us live, includes this level of bias?


Deliberately placed right after the Springdale/COFA material, in the “closer to home” slot — this is not a distant case study, it’s happening in Honolulu and across the state where (presumably) most students live. Handle with care: name the documented facts (the 2019 USCCR report, the Korab v. Fink Medicaid case, the COVID-19 case data, the UH Mānoa study). Note the COVID figures are for all Pacific Islanders, not Micronesians alone; Hawai’i DOH and the 2021 Hawai’i Advisory Committee report discuss COFA migrants specifically, including that Micronesians were overrepresented among cases and in COVID-order arrests. Likely contributing factors reported: crowded multigenerational housing, frontline jobs (hotels, airport, food service), and limited insurance access rather than generalizing about “Hawai’i locals” as a monolith, and don’t let the discussion collapse into guilt — the aim is awareness and connecting it back to the language-vitality themes from the rest of the lecture (the same communities whose languages we just spent an hour on are the ones facing this). If any FAS/Micronesian students are in the room, be mindful they may have lived experience here — don’t put anyone on the spot to represent “the community.”

title: The Languages of Micronesia
text:
Exit Ticket (4 min)
Write silently; we’ll collect these on the way out.

If your family or community had to relocate entirely to a new country, what part of your language or culture do you think would survive the move, and what might not?


~4 min, silent writing. Direct callback to today’s Kiribati relocation discussion and the Springdale diaspora slide — personalizes the same question Kiribati and Marshallese communities are actually facing.
